posts.title: How to Become a Notary Public in Florida
posts.metaTitle: How to Become a Notary Public in Florida (2026 Requirements, Cost & Steps)
posts.metaDesc: Step-by-step requirements to become a Florida notary public in 2026: eligibility, the $7,500 bond, education, application, fees, and how long a commission lasts.
keywords: how to become a notary in florida
posts.excerpt: Florida commissions notaries for four-year terms. Here is exactly what the state requires, what it costs, and how long it takes.

sections.html:
Under Fla. Stat. §117.01(1), an applicant for a Florida notary commission must be at least 18 years old, be a legal resident of the State of Florida, and be able to read, write, and understand the English language.

The statute also requires the application to include the applicant's full name, residence address and telephone number, business address and telephone number, date of birth, and Social Security number. The Social Security number is confidential and exempt from public disclosure under §119.071(5)(a) — it never appears in the public commission record.

An applicant who is not a United States citizen must record a declaration of domicile.

There are three separate costs, and people routinely confuse them.

  • The state filing fee — paid to the Florida Department of State with the application.
  • The $7,500 surety bond — required by §117.01(6). This is not insurance for you. A surety bond pays the public if you make an error, and the surety can then come after you for reimbursement.
  • Errors & omissions insurance — not required by Florida law. E&O is what actually protects the notary. It is optional for a general commission, but it is effectively mandatory if you want signing work, because signing services and title companies set their own minimums.

Most applicants go through a bonding agency, which bundles the bond, the education, the application filing, and a seal into one package. That is why you see quoted prices that bear no relation to the state fee alone.

First-time applicants must complete a state-approved notary education course before applying. Renewing notaries are treated differently from first-time applicants — confirm your current obligation with the Department of State or your bonding agency rather than assuming.

Applications are submitted to the Florida Department of State through a bonding agency. The state issues the commission certificate; the bonding agency typically supplies the seal.

A Florida notary commission runs for four years. Your expiration date appears on your commission and in the public record — you can look up any Florida notary, including yourself, in this register or directly through the Department of State.

Renewal is not automatic. Start roughly 90 days out; a lapse means reapplying rather than renewing, and it takes any Remote Online Notary registration down with it.

Florida caps the fee for the notarial act itself at $10 per act (§117.05) and $25 per online notarization (§117.275). Those caps apply only to the act. Travel, printing, and signing-agent service fees are separate, uncapped, and negotiated directly. That distinction is the entire economics of mobile and loan-signing work — see what a Florida notary can charge.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to become a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: There are three separate costs: the state filing fee paid to the Florida Department of State, the mandatory $7,500 surety bond required by Fla. Stat. 117.01(6), and optional errors and omissions insurance. Most applicants buy a bundled package from a bonding agency that includes the bond, education, filing, and seal.

faqs.q: How long does a Florida notary commission last?
faqs.a: Four years. Renewal is not automatic, and a lapsed commission must be reapplied for rather than renewed. A lapse also terminates any Remote Online Notary registration.

faqs.q: Do I need errors and omissions insurance to be a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida law requires a $7,500 surety bond but does not require E&O insurance. However, signing services and title companies set their own E&O minimums, so it is practically necessary for anyone seeking loan signing work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a notary bond and E&O insurance?
faqs.a: A surety bond protects the public. If you make an error, the bond pays the injured party and the surety can seek reimbursement from you. E&O insurance protects you, covering your own defense and liability for unintentional mistakes.

faqs.q: Can a non-US citizen become a Florida notary?
faqs.a: Yes. A permanent resident who is not a United States citizen may be appointed, but must record a declaration of domicile.

posts.title: How Much Can a Florida Notary Charge?
posts.metaTitle: How Much Can a Florida Notary Charge? Fees, Caps & Travel Costs (2026)
posts.metaDesc: Florida caps notarial acts at $10 and online notarizations at $25. Travel and signing fees are uncapped. Here is what a notary may legally charge and why mobile notaries cost more.
keywords: how much does a notary cost in florida
posts.excerpt: The statutory cap is $10 per act. So why does a mobile notary quote $75? Because the cap covers the act, not the trip.

sections.html:
Florida sets a hard ceiling on the fee for the notarial act itself:

  • $10 per notarial act for traditional, in-person notarization — Fla. Stat. §117.05(2)(a)
  • $25 per notarial act performed by remote online notarization — Fla. Stat. §117.275

An "act" is a single notarization — one acknowledgment, one jurat, one oath. A document requiring three notarizations may be charged three times.

This is where nearly all confusion originates. The caps apply to the notarial act. They do not apply to:

  • Travel — a mobile notary coming to your home, hospital, or office
  • Printing — loan packages routinely run 100–200 pages, often on two paper sizes
  • Signing-agent services — walking a borrower through a closing package, checking completeness, shipping the return
  • After-hours and weekend availability
  • Scanbacks and courier or shipping charges

These are ordinary contract fees negotiated between you and the notary. Florida does not regulate them.

A mobile notary quoting $75 to visit your home for one signature is not overcharging. They are charging $10 for the act and $65 for the trip, and they are entitled to do so — provided the fees are disclosed to you in advance.

A loan signing agent handling a refinance package typically charges $85–$200. That covers printing the package, travelling to the borrower, sitting through a 45–90 minute signing, and shipping the documents back — with only the notarizations themselves subject to the statutory cap.

Ask for the total in advance and get it in writing. A notary should be able to break the quote into the act fee and everything else. A notary may not charge for the act beyond the cap, and may not condition the notarization on buying another service.

Also worth knowing: a notary cannot give you legal advice, choose your document, or explain its legal effect. That is the practice of law. If the notary is telling you what a document means for your situation, something is wrong.

faqs.q: How much can a notary charge in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida caps the notarial act at $10 per act under Fla. Stat. 117.05(2)(a), and at $25 per act for remote online notarization under Fla. Stat. 117.275. Travel, printing, and signing-agent service fees are not capped and are negotiated separately.

faqs.q: Why do mobile notaries charge $75 or more in Florida?
faqs.a: Because the $10 cap applies only to the notarial act. Travel to your location is a separate, uncapped service fee. A $75 quote is typically $10 for the act and $65 for travel and convenience.

faqs.q: How much does a loan signing agent charge in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically $85 to $200 per signing, depending on the loan product. That covers printing a 100 to 200 page package, travel, conducting the signing, and shipping documents back. Only the notarizations themselves are capped at $10 each.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary charge more than $10 per signature?
faqs.a: Not for the notarial act itself. A notary may charge separately for travel, printing, and other services, but the act is capped at $10, or $25 for an online notarization.

faqs.q: Does a notary have to tell me the fee in advance?
faqs.a: You should always ask for the total in writing before the appointment, itemized between the notarial act fee and any travel or service charges.

posts.title: Remote Online Notarization (RON) in Florida
posts.metaTitle: Remote Online Notarization in Florida: How RON Works & How to Register (2026)
posts.metaDesc: How remote online notarization works in Florida, what it costs, the $25,000 RON bond and E&O requirement, and how a notary registers under Fla. Stat. 117.225.
keywords: how to become a remote online notary in florida
posts.excerpt: Florida was among the first states to authorize RON. Here is how a session actually works, and what a notary must do to offer it.

sections.html:
Remote Online Notarization lets a notary and a signer complete a notarization over live audio-video from different locations. It is authorised in Florida under Chapter 117, Part II. The signer's identity is confirmed through credential analysis and knowledge-based authentication, the entire session is recorded, and the recording is retained.

RON is not the same as emailing a scanned document to a notary. It is a live, recorded, identity-verified session on an approved platform.

Three formats get conflated constantly:

  • Traditional — paper document, wet ink signature, physical seal, everyone in the same room.
  • IPEN (in-person electronic notarization) — everyone is still in the same room, but the document and signatures are electronic. Authorised by §117.021, and it requires no separate registration beyond your standard commission. §117.021(4) gives the notary the right to select the technology.
  • RON — the signer is remote, appearing by audio-video. This requires separate registration with the Department of State.

The difference that matters: remote means registration; electronic-but-in-person does not.

sections.h: What a notary needs to offer RON
sections.html:
Under §117.225, a Florida notary registering as an online notary public must:

  • Hold a current traditional notary commission
  • Complete a state-approved RON education course
  • Obtain a separate $25,000 surety bond — this is in addition to the $7,500 traditional bond
  • Carry errors & omissions insurance of at least $25,000
  • Register with the Department of State and pay the filing fee
  • Use a Department-registered RON technology provider

The trap: your RON registration expires on the same day as your underlying notary commission, regardless of when you registered it. There is no grace period. If your commission lapses, you reapply as a notary and then reapply for RON from scratch.

A Florida notary may charge up to $25 per online notarial act under §117.275 — higher than the $10 traditional cap, reflecting the platform and retention costs. Travel is irrelevant for RON, but platform fees, document handling, and signing-agent services remain separate and uncapped.

Not everything can be done remotely. Certain documents and county recording practices still require wet signatures, and in real estate the lender and title underwriter decide the format per file — not the notary and not the signer.

faqs.q: Is remote online notarization legal in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Florida authorises remote online notarization under Chapter 117, Part II of the Florida Statutes. The notary must be separately registered as an online notary public with the Florida Department of State.

faqs.q: How much does a remote online notarization cost in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida caps the online notarial act at $25 under Fla. Stat. 117.275, compared to $10 for a traditional act. Platform fees and any signing-agent services are separate and not capped.

faqs.q: What does a Florida notary need to perform remote online notarizations?
faqs.a: A current traditional commission, a state-approved RON education course, a separate $25,000 surety bond, at least $25,000 in errors and omissions insurance, registration with the Department of State, and use of a registered RON technology provider.

faqs.q: Does a Florida RON registration expire with the notary commission?
faqs.a: Yes. The online notary registration expires on the same day as the underlying notary commission regardless of when it was filed, and there is no grace period. If the commission lapses, both must be applied for again.

faqs.q: What is the difference between RON and IPEN?
faqs.a: RON means the signer appears remotely by audio-video and requires separate state registration. IPEN, in-person electronic notarization, means everyone is physically present but the document and signature are electronic. IPEN is authorised under Fla. Stat. 117.021 and requires no separate registration.

posts.title: How to Become a Loan Signing Agent in Florida
posts.metaTitle: How to Become a Loan Signing Agent in Florida (2026): Steps, Cost & Earnings
posts.metaDesc: What a notary signing agent actually does, the background screening and E&O that platforms require, realistic per-signing fees in Florida, and how to get assigned work.

how much do loan signing agents make
posts.excerpt: A loan signing agent is a notary who handles mortgage closing packages. The commission is the easy part; the credentials are what gate the work.

sections.html:
A notary signing agent presents a mortgage closing package to a borrower, directs them where to sign and date, performs the notarizations, and returns the executed package to the title company or lender. A typical refinance package runs 100–200 pages and takes 45–90 minutes at the table.

What the job is not: giving advice. A signing agent may identify a document by name and point to where it is signed. Explaining what a term means for the borrower's situation, or advising whether they should sign, is the unauthorised practice of law.

sections.h: What you need beyond the commission
sections.html:
The Florida commission is the entry ticket. The work is gated by what the platforms and title companies require on top:

  • A current background screening. Most platforms require one completed within the last 12 months. This is the single most common reason applications sit unprocessed.
  • Errors & omissions insurance. Not required by Florida law, but effectively mandatory. Coverage of $25,000 is a common floor; $100,000 clears essentially every published threshold, and some platforms require it for real estate work specifically.
  • A signing agent certification. Not a legal requirement. Many title companies filter for it.
  • A dual-tray laser printer. Loan packages print on both letter and legal paper. This is not optional equipment.
  • A scanner for same-day scanbacks.

Realistic per-signing fees, depending on product and market:

  • Refinance — $85–$150
  • Purchase, buyer package — $100–$200
  • Seller-only — $75–$125
  • Reverse mortgage — $125–$275 (highest liability; never accept refinance pricing)
  • Loan modification — $50–$125

Subtract printing, toner, paper, mileage, and shipping. Net is meaningfully lower than gross, and volume depends entirely on interest rates.

Assignments come from signing services and title companies, not from consumer directories. A directory listing produces general notary work — a $10 acknowledgment plus a travel fee — not loan closings.

Loan signing work is dispatched. You register with signing service platforms, they send you assignments, and they keep a spread. Separately, independent title companies and closing law firms maintain their own lists of notaries they call directly, which is where the better fees are.

If you are a Florida notary looking for signing assignments, RON Closing dispatches both remote online sessions and in-person signings to commissioned Florida notaries.

faqs.q: How much do loan signing agents make in Florida?
faqs.a: Per-signing fees typically range from $85 to $150 for a refinance, $100 to $200 for a purchase package, and $125 to $275 for a reverse mortgage. Printing, toner, mileage, and shipping come out of that, and volume depends heavily on interest rates.

faqs.q: Do you need a certification to be a loan signing agent in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida law requires only a notary commission. However, most signing services and title companies require a background screening completed within the last 12 months, errors and omissions insurance, and often a signing agent certification before assigning work.

faqs.q: How much E&O insurance does a loan signing agent need?
faqs.a: Florida does not require any. In practice, $25,000 is a common minimum among signing platforms, and $100,000 clears essentially every published threshold. Some platforms require $100,000 specifically for real estate signings.

faqs.q: Can a notary signing agent explain loan documents to a borrower?
faqs.a: No. A signing agent may identify a document by name and indicate where to sign. Explaining what a document means for the borrower's situation, or advising whether to sign, is the unauthorised practice of law.

faqs.q: Do I need a special printer to be a loan signing agent?
faqs.a: Yes, practically speaking. Loan packages print on both letter and legal size paper, so a dual-tray laser printer is standard equipment, along with a scanner for same-day scanbacks.

posts.title: Florida Deed Witness Requirements
posts.metaTitle: Do Florida Deeds Need Witnesses? Two-Witness Rule Explained (Fla. Stat. 689.01)
posts.metaDesc: Florida deeds require two subscribing witnesses under Fla. Stat. 689.01. Mortgages do not. Here is the difference, and when a notary may serve as one of the witnesses.
keywords: do deeds need witnesses in florida
can a notary be a witness in florida
posts.excerpt: Deeds need two witnesses. Mortgages do not. Getting this wrong is the most common Florida closing error there is.

sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §689.01 requires that a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses. A deed executed without them is defective and can create serious title problems.

This applies to deeds — warranty deeds, quit claim deeds, and similar instruments conveying an interest in land.

A mortgage does not carry the same statutory witness requirement. Under §697.02, a Florida mortgage is a lien on property, not a conveyance of a freehold estate, and §695.26(1)(f) expressly exempts mortgages from the witness-signature requirement for recording. Fannie Mae's Florida security instrument now treats the witness lines as optional for exactly this reason.

But follow the closing instructions, not the statute. Virtually every Florida lender still prints two witness lines on the mortgage, and the title company's instructions require them completed. An unusable loan file is an unusable loan file regardless of what the statute permits.

sections.h: Can the notary be a witness?
sections.html:
In Florida, yes — but only if the notary actually observed the signer sign. The notary signs twice: once on a witness line, once in the notarial certificate.

The condition matters. A notary who merely takes an acknowledgment — where the signer confirms a signature they made earlier, outside the notary's presence — did not witness the signing and cannot serve as a subscribing witness to it.

You still need a second, independent witness either way. A witness should not be a party to the transaction or have a financial interest in it.

Witnesses may also appear remotely by audio-video under §689.01(2)–(3).

Confirm the witness requirement in writing with the title company before any purchase or seller signing. Ask specifically: how many witnesses, and may the notary serve as one. Ten seconds of email saves a re-draw.

Note that leases no longer require witnesses following the 2020 amendment to §689.01.

faqs.q: Do deeds need to be witnessed in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Fla. Stat. 689.01 requires a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property to be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses. A deed executed without them is defective.

faqs.q: Do Florida mortgages require witnesses?
faqs.a: Not statutorily. A mortgage is a lien rather than a conveyance under Fla. Stat. 697.02, and Fla. Stat. 695.26(1)(f) exempts mortgages from the witness requirement for recording. However, most lenders still print witness lines and closing instructions typically require them completed.

faqs.q: Can a notary be a witness in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes, if the notary actually observed the signer sign the document. The notary signs twice, once as a witness and once in the notarial certificate. A notary who only takes an acknowledgment of a signature made earlier did not witness the signing and cannot serve as a subscribing witness.

faqs.q: How many witnesses does a Florida deed need?
faqs.a: Two subscribing witnesses. If the notary personally observed the signing and serves as one, a second independent witness is still required.

faqs.q: Do leases need witnesses in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida amended Fla. Stat. 689.01 in 2020 to remove the two-witness requirement for leases.

posts.title: How to Renew a Florida Notary Commission
posts.metaTitle: How to Renew a Florida Notary Commission (2026): Timeline, Cost & What Lapses
posts.metaDesc: When to start renewing a Florida notary commission, what it costs, what happens if it lapses, and why a lapse also terminates your Remote Online Notary registration.
posts.excerpt: A Florida commission runs four years and does not renew itself. Letting it lapse costs more than renewing on time.

sections.html:
A Florida notary commission runs four years from the date of issue. Renewal is not automatic and the state does not guarantee a reminder.

Begin roughly 90 days before expiration. That leaves room for the bond, any required education, processing, and delivery of a new seal without a gap in your authority to notarize.

You can confirm your own expiration date in this register or through the Department of State.

Renewal broadly mirrors the original application: a new $7,500 surety bond for the new four-year term under §117.01(6), a renewal application filed with the Department of State, the filing fee, and a new seal reflecting the new commission number and expiration date.

Education obligations differ between first-time applicants and renewing notaries. Confirm your current requirement rather than assuming it carries over.

sections.h: What happens if you let it lapse
sections.html:
There is no grace period. Once the commission expires you are not a notary, and any notarization performed after that date is invalid.

A lapse means reapplying as a new notary rather than renewing — which may pull in first-time education requirements.

The expensive part: a lapsed commission also terminates your Remote Online Notary registration. RON registration expires on the same day as the underlying commission regardless of when it was filed. Restoring RON means redoing the course, the separate $25,000 RON bond, the $25,000 E&O, and the registration from scratch.

sections.h: Renew the commission early if you hold RON
sections.html:
Because RON registration inherits the commission's expiration date, registering for RON late in a commission term buys you only the remainder of that term.

If you plan to offer remote online notarization, it is usually worth renewing the underlying commission first, so the RON registration rides a fresh four-year term instead of expiring in a few months.

faqs.q: How do I renew my Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: File a renewal application with the Florida Department of State, obtain a new $7,500 surety bond for the new four-year term, pay the filing fee, and get a new seal showing the new commission number and expiration date. Start about 90 days before expiration.

faqs.q: What happens if my Florida notary commission expires?
faqs.a: There is no grace period. You are no longer a notary and any notarization performed after expiration is invalid. You must reapply as a new notary rather than renew, which may trigger first-time education requirements.

faqs.q: Does my RON registration expire when my notary commission expires?
faqs.a: Yes. A Florida Remote Online Notary registration expires on the same day as the underlying notary commission, regardless of when the RON registration was filed. There is no grace period, and restoring it requires redoing the course, the $25,000 RON bond, the E&O coverage, and the registration.

faqs.q: How long is a Florida notary commission valid?
faqs.a: Four years from the date of issue.

faqs.q: Should I renew my commission early if I want to offer RON?
faqs.a: Often yes. Because RON registration inherits the commission's expiration date, registering late in a term gives you only the remaining months. Renewing the commission first lets the RON registration ride a fresh four-year term.

posts.title: What Is a Mobile Notary?
posts.metaTitle: What Is a Mobile Notary? What They Do, What They Cost & When to Use One
posts.metaDesc: A mobile notary travels to you. Here is what they can and cannot do, what they charge in Florida, and when a mobile notary is the right choice over a bank or shipping store.
posts.excerpt: A mobile notary is a commissioned notary who comes to you. The notarial act is the same; you are paying for the travel.

sections.html:
A mobile notary is a commissioned notary public who travels to the signer — a home, hospital, care facility, office, jail, or coffee shop — rather than requiring the signer to come to them.

The notarial act is identical to one performed at a bank. The notary verifies identity, witnesses the signature or takes the acknowledgment, completes the certificate, and applies the seal. What differs is convenience.

• Hospital and care facility signings — powers of attorney, advance directives, healthcare surrogate designations for someone who cannot travel
  • Real estate closings outside a title office, or after hours
  • Estate documents — wills, trusts, deeds where multiple signers and witnesses must be assembled
  • Time-sensitive documents after banks have closed
  • Multiple signers in one place, where bringing everyone to a branch is impractical

Florida caps the notarial act at $10 (§117.05). Travel is not capped. A typical mobile notary quote in Florida runs $40–$100 depending on distance, time of day, and number of documents — $10 of which is the act, the rest travel and convenience.

That is entirely lawful, provided the fee is disclosed to you beforehand. Ask for the total in writing, itemized. See what a Florida notary can charge.

sections.h: What a mobile notary cannot do
sections.html:
This matters more than most people realise. A Florida notary may not:

  • Give legal advice or explain what a document means for your situation
  • Choose or prepare a document for you
  • Notarize a signature when the signer is not present
  • Notarize their own signature, or a document in which they have a financial interest
  • Certify a copy of a vital record such as a birth or death certificate

If a notary is advising you on what to sign, that is the practice of law, and they should not be doing it.

You can search this register by county, city, or ZIP code for commissioned Florida notaries. Every entry shows the commission number and expiration date so you can verify it independently with the Department of State before your appointment.

faqs.q: What is a mobile notary?
faqs.a: A mobile notary is a commissioned notary public who travels to the signer's location rather than requiring the signer to come to an office. The notarial act itself is identical to one performed at a bank.

faqs.q: How much does a mobile notary cost in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically $40 to $100. Florida caps the notarial act at $10, but travel and convenience fees are not capped and make up the rest. The fee should be disclosed in advance.

faqs.q: Can a mobile notary come to a hospital?
faqs.a: Yes. Hospital and care facility signings are among the most common uses for a mobile notary, particularly for powers of attorney, advance directives, and healthcare surrogate designations.

faqs.q: Can a notary tell me what my document means?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect or advising whether to sign is the practice of law. A Florida notary may identify a document by name and indicate where to sign, and nothing more.

faqs.q: Can a notary certify a copy of a birth certificate in Florida?
faqs.a: No. A Florida notary may not certify copies of vital records such as birth or death certificates. Certified copies must be obtained from the issuing agency.

posts.excerpt: Directories and signing services are different businesses. Confusing them is why notaries pay for listings that never produce work.

sections.html:
Notaries routinely pay for the wrong product because these are used interchangeably. They are not the same.

A directory is consumer-facing. Members of the public search it and contact the notary directly. It produces general notary work — a $10 acknowledgment plus a travel fee. Notaries pay to be listed or to be placed higher.

A signing service is business-facing and largely invisible to the public. Title companies and lenders place orders; the platform dispatches them to notaries and keeps a spread. It produces loan signings at $85–$200. Registration is generally free; the platform is paid from the spread.

The practical consequence: a directory listing will not get you loan signing work. If your goal is closings, register with signing services. If your goal is local walk-in work, a directory helps.

Published rates across the established notary directories generally fall between roughly $79 and $500 per year, depending on placement and market. Common structures include a flat annual membership, tiered placement positions, per-county add-ons, and premium top-of-page slots priced by how competitive the market is.

Worth knowing before you buy: several long-standing directories are widely reported by working notaries to produce little assignment volume. Ask for traffic or lead figures before paying for placement, and be sceptical of any directory that will not provide them.

• Does listing cost anything? A directory that charges for basic inclusion has a smaller database, which means less traffic, which means fewer leads.
  • Is the data verified? Listings built from state commission records can be checked against the issuing authority. Self-reported listings cannot.
  • Can you see the fee structure before signing up?
  • Does it produce actual work, or only visibility? These are different promises.
  • Can you remove yourself easily?

State Notary Agent is a free public directory of commissioned Florida notaries, built from Florida Department of State commission records. Basic inclusion costs nothing and searching costs nothing. Notaries may claim an entry at no charge to add services and contact details, and optional paid placement is published openly on the rate card.

It is not a signing service and does not dispatch loan closings. Florida notaries seeking signing assignments — remote online sessions or in-person appointments — should look to RON Closing, which dispatches both to commissioned Florida notaries.

posts.metaTitle: Notary Bond vs E&O Insurance: What's the Difference? (Florida 2026)
posts.metaDesc: A surety bond protects the public; E&O insurance protects the notary. Florida requires a $7,500 bond and does not require E&O. Here is why you likely need both.
posts.excerpt: Florida requires one and not the other. Most notaries misunderstand which protects them.

sections.html:
Florida requires a $7,500 surety bond under Fla. Stat. §117.01(6). A surety bond is not insurance for you. It is a financial guarantee to the public.

If you make a notarial error that harms someone, the surety pays the injured party up to the bond amount — and then has the right to seek reimbursement from you. You are ultimately on the hook.

Errors & omissions insurance protects the notary. It covers your legal defence and your liability for unintentional mistakes, up to the policy limit, without a right of reimbursement against you.

Florida does not require E&O. It is optional as a matter of law. But signing services and title companies set their own minimums, so it is practically mandatory for anyone doing loan work — $25,000 is a common floor and $100,000 clears essentially every published threshold.

If you register for remote online notarization, §117.225 requires a separate $25,000 surety bond plus at least $25,000 in E&O. These are in addition to the $7,500 traditional bond, not a replacement for it.

So a Florida notary offering RON carries two bonds and a mandatory E&O policy.

faqs.q: Does Florida require notaries to have E&O insurance?
faqs.a: No. Florida requires a $7,500 surety bond under Fla. Stat. 117.01(6) but does not require errors and omissions insurance for a traditional commission. E&O becomes mandatory in practice because signing services and title companies set their own minimums.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a notary bond and E&O insurance?
faqs.a: A surety bond protects the public and the surety can seek reimbursement from the notary after paying a claim. E&O insurance protects the notary, covering defence and liability for unintentional errors without recourse against you.

faqs.q: How much E&O insurance should a Florida notary carry?
faqs.a: $25,000 is a common minimum among signing platforms. $100,000 clears essentially every published requirement, and some platforms require $100,000 specifically for real estate signings.

faqs.q: Does remote online notarization require a separate bond in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Fla. Stat. 117.225 requires a separate $25,000 surety bond and at least $25,000 in E&O coverage, in addition to the $7,500 traditional notary bond.

posts.title: What Does a Notary Public Do?
posts.metaTitle: What Does a Notary Public Do? Duties, Limits & Types of Notarial Acts
posts.metaDesc: A notary verifies identity and witnesses signatures — they do not verify that a document is true or legal. Here is what a notary actually does, and what they may never do.
posts.excerpt: A notary is an impartial witness to identity — not a reviewer of your document.

sections.html:
A notary public is a state-commissioned impartial witness. The notary's job is to verify who signed a document — not what the document says, whether it is accurate, or whether it is a good idea.

A notary confirms the signer's identity, confirms they are signing willingly and appear aware of what they are doing, completes a notarial certificate, and applies a seal.

• Acknowledgment — the signer confirms the signature is theirs and was made voluntarily. The signature may have been made earlier, outside the notary's presence.
  • Jurat — the signer swears or affirms the contents are true, and must sign in front of the notary.
  • Oath or affirmation — administered on its own, as for a sworn statement.
  • Attested copy — certifying a photocopy matches an original, subject to limits.
  • Solemnizing marriage — Florida is one of the few states where notaries may perform marriages.

The distinction between an acknowledgment and a jurat matters: only a jurat requires the signature to be made in the notary's presence.

sections.h: What a notary may never do
sections.html:
• Give legal advice, choose your document, or explain its legal effect
  • Notarize a signature when the signer is not physically or, for RON, virtually present
  • Notarize their own signature or a document they have a financial interest in
  • Certify a copy of a vital record such as a birth, death, or marriage certificate
  • Notarize a document with blank spaces

If a notary is telling you what your document means for your situation, that is the unauthorised practice of law.

faqs.q: What does a notary public actually do?
faqs.a: A notary is a state-commissioned impartial witness who verifies the identity of a signer, confirms they are signing willingly, completes a notarial certificate, and applies a seal. A notary does not verify that a document is accurate, legal, or advisable.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an acknowledgment and a jurat?
faqs.a: In an acknowledgment, the signer confirms the signature is theirs and was made voluntarily; it may have been signed earlier outside the notary's presence. In a jurat, the signer swears the contents are true and must sign in front of the notary.

faqs.q: Can a notary give legal advice?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect, choosing a document, or advising whether to sign is the practice of law and is prohibited for notaries who are not attorneys.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary perform a marriage?
faqs.a: Yes. Florida is one of a small number of states where a notary public may solemnize a marriage.

posts.title: What ID Do You Need for a Notary?
posts.metaTitle: What ID Do You Need for a Notary? Accepted Identification in Florida
posts.metaDesc: What identification a Florida notary can accept, what happens if you have no ID, and how credible witnesses work under Fla. Stat. 117.05.
keywords: what id do you need for a notary
posts.excerpt: Bring a current government photo ID. If you don't have one, there is a legal alternative.

sections.html:
Florida law at §117.05(5) sets out how a notary establishes a signer's identity. In practice a notary will ask for a current, government-issued photo identification — a driver licence, state ID card, passport, or military ID.

The document must be current and must bear a photograph and signature. Expired identification is generally not acceptable.

A notary may also rely on personal knowledge of the signer — meaning the notary actually knows the person, not that they met them in the lobby ten minutes ago. This is a real legal standard, not a courtesy.

If you have no acceptable identification, Florida permits identification through credible witnesses. A credible witness personally knows you, swears to your identity, and must themselves be identified by the notary.

The witness cannot have a financial interest in the document and cannot be named in it. Requirements are specific, so tell the notary in advance if you will need this route — it changes who needs to be in the room.

faqs.q: What ID do I need to get something notarized in Florida?
faqs.a: A current government-issued photo identification such as a driver licence, state ID card, passport, or military ID. It must bear a photograph and signature and must not be expired.

faqs.q: Can I get something notarized without ID?
faqs.a: Possibly. Florida permits identification through credible witnesses who personally know you, swear to your identity, and are themselves identified by the notary. A notary may also rely on personal knowledge if they genuinely know you.

faqs.q: Will a notary accept an expired ID?
faqs.a: Generally no. Identification is normally required to be current.

faqs.q: Can a credible witness be a family member?
faqs.a: A credible witness must personally know the signer, must not have a financial interest in the document, and must not be named in it. Whether a particular relative qualifies depends on those conditions.

posts.title: How to Get a Document Notarized
posts.metaTitle: How to Get a Document Notarized in Florida: Steps, Cost & What to Bring
posts.metaDesc: What to bring, what it costs, where to go, and the mistakes that get people turned away at the notary appointment.
keywords: how to get a document notarized
posts.excerpt: Most failed notary appointments fail for the same three reasons. All are avoidable.

sections.html:
• The complete document — unsigned, unless the act is an acknowledgment
  • Current government photo ID for every signer
  • Every signer, physically present
  • Any required witnesses — ask in advance whether the document needs them

Do not sign in advance unless you have confirmed the act is an acknowledgment. A jurat requires you to sign in front of the notary, and signing early means starting over.

Banks and credit unions often notarise for account holders. Shipping and print shops commonly offer it. Public libraries and county offices sometimes do.

A mobile notary travels to you — useful for hospitals, care facilities, after-hours signings, or when several signers must be assembled. A remote online notary can complete the notarization by live video if the document and recipient permit it.

You can search this register for commissioned Florida notaries by county, city, or ZIP.

• Blank spaces. A notary cannot notarise a document with blanks. Fill everything in first.
  • Signer not present. No exceptions, and no, you cannot bring the document in for someone else.
  • Expired or missing ID.
  • Wrong or missing certificate wording. If the document lacks notarial wording, the notary may need you to choose which act you need — and they cannot choose for you, because that would be legal advice.

faqs.q: What do I need to bring to get a document notarized?
faqs.a: The complete document with no blank spaces, current government photo ID for every signer, all signers present in person, and any witnesses the document requires.

faqs.q: Should I sign the document before seeing the notary?
faqs.a: Not unless you have confirmed the act is an acknowledgment. A jurat requires you to sign in the notary's presence, so signing early means the document must be redone.

faqs.q: Where can I get a document notarized in Florida?
faqs.a: Banks and credit unions often notarise for account holders, and shipping and print shops commonly offer it. A mobile notary will travel to you, and a remote online notary can complete it by live video if the recipient accepts it.

faqs.q: Can a notary notarize a document with blank spaces?
faqs.a: No. Blank spaces must be completed or struck through before notarization.

posts.title: What Documents Need to Be Notarized?
posts.metaTitle: What Documents Need to Be Notarized? Common Types Explained
posts.metaDesc: Deeds, powers of attorney, affidavits, and more — which documents typically require notarization, and which people wrongly assume do.
keywords: what documents need to be notarized
does a will need to be notarized
posts.excerpt: Notarization is required far less often than people assume — but where it is required, skipping it can void the document.

sections.html:
• Deeds and real property conveyances — and in Florida, also two subscribing witnesses under §689.01
  • Mortgages and loan documents
  • Powers of attorney
  • Affidavits and sworn statements
  • Advance directives and healthcare surrogate designations
  • Trust documents
  • Vehicle title transfers in some circumstances
  • Parental consent for a minor's travel

Ordinary contracts usually do not require notarization. A signed contract is generally binding without it. Notarization is sometimes added for evidentiary weight, not validity.

Wills are a special case. In Florida a will is executed with witnesses; notarization is associated with making it self-proving, which simplifies probate. Requirements are technical and getting them wrong has serious consequences — this is squarely a question for an attorney, not a notary.

sections.h: How to find out for certain
sections.html:
The document itself usually tells you. If it has a notarial certificate block — wording beginning "State of Florida, County of ___" with a space for a seal — it is meant to be notarized.

If you are unsure, ask the receiving party: the bank, the county recorder, the court, the agency. They set the requirement. A notary cannot tell you whether your document needs notarization, because that would be legal advice.

faqs.q: What documents need to be notarized?
faqs.a: Commonly: deeds and property conveyances, mortgages, powers of attorney, affidavits and sworn statements, advance directives, trust documents, some vehicle title transfers, and parental travel consent forms.

faqs.q: Do contracts need to be notarized?
faqs.a: Usually not. A signed contract is generally binding without notarization. Notarization is sometimes added for evidentiary weight rather than validity.

faqs.q: Does a will need to be notarized in Florida?
faqs.a: A Florida will is executed with witnesses. Notarization is associated with making a will self-proving, which simplifies probate. The requirements are technical and should be confirmed with an attorney.

faqs.q: How do I know if my document needs notarization?
faqs.a: Check whether the document contains a notarial certificate block. If unsure, ask the receiving party — the bank, county recorder, court, or agency — since they set the requirement. A notary cannot advise you on this.

posts.title: Notarizing a Power of Attorney in Florida
posts.metaTitle: Power of Attorney Notarization in Florida: Witnesses & Requirements
posts.metaDesc: Florida powers of attorney require notarization and two witnesses. Here is how execution works and what commonly goes wrong.
posts.excerpt: A Florida POA needs more than a notary — and the most common failure is assembling the wrong people.

sections.html:
Under Fla. Stat. Chapter 709, a Florida power of attorney must be signed by the principal in the presence of two subscribing witnesses and must be acknowledged before a notary public.

That means three people beyond the principal: two witnesses and the notary. A notary alone is not sufficient, and this is by far the most common reason a POA signing has to be repeated.

sections.h: Can the notary be a witness?
sections.html:
In Florida a notary may generally serve as one of the two subscribing witnesses, provided they actually observed the principal sign and are not a party to or interested in the instrument. You still need a second, independent witness.

Because a POA is a high-stakes instrument, many practitioners prefer two independent witnesses plus a separate notary. Confirm with the attorney who drafted it.

A notary must be satisfied the principal is signing willingly and appears aware of what they are doing. A notary is not a doctor and does not assess legal capacity — but a notary who has genuine doubt should decline.

This comes up constantly in hospital and care-facility signings. If capacity is genuinely in question, that is a matter for the attorney and the treating physician, not the notary.

faqs.q: Does a power of attorney need to be notarized in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes. Under Fla. Stat. Chapter 709, a Florida power of attorney must be signed by the principal in the presence of two subscribing witnesses and acknowledged before a notary public.

faqs.q: How many witnesses does a Florida power of attorney need?
faqs.a: Two subscribing witnesses, in addition to notarization.

faqs.q: Can the notary act as a witness on a Florida power of attorney?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if the notary actually observed the principal sign and has no interest in the instrument. A second independent witness is still required. Many practitioners prefer two independent witnesses plus a separate notary.

faqs.q: Can a notary refuse to notarize a power of attorney?
faqs.a: Yes. A notary who has genuine doubt that the principal is signing willingly or appears aware of what they are doing should decline. A notary does not assess legal capacity but is not required to proceed despite real doubt.

posts.title: Can a Notary Refuse to Notarize?
posts.metaTitle: Can a Notary Refuse to Notarize? Lawful Reasons to Decline
posts.metaDesc: When a Florida notary may — and must — refuse a notarization, and when refusing would be improper.
keywords: can a notary refuse to notarize
posts.excerpt: Yes, and sometimes they are required to. Here is where the line sits.

sections.html:
• The signer is not present. No exceptions.
  • Identity cannot be established. No acceptable ID, no personal knowledge, no credible witness.
  • The signer does not appear to be acting willingly, or appears not to understand what they are signing.
  • The document contains blank spaces.
  • The notary has a financial interest in the transaction, or is a party to it.
  • The signer cannot communicate with the notary directly — a notary generally may not rely on a translator to establish the signer's understanding.

A notary may decline for reasons of practicality — being outside their service area, unavailable, or uncomfortable with a transaction that looks irregular. A notary is not obliged to accept every request.

What a notary may not do is decline on the basis of race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, or similar protected characteristics.

Ask specifically why. Most refusals come down to a fixable problem: missing signer, expired ID, a blank field, or a missing witness. Fix it and return.

If the refusal is because the notary suspects the signing is not voluntary, that is the system working. Pressuring another notary to proceed is a poor idea.

faqs.q: Can a notary refuse to notarize a document?
faqs.a: Yes. A notary must decline when the signer is not present, identity cannot be established, the signer does not appear to be acting willingly or aware, the document has blank spaces, or the notary has a financial interest. A notary may also decline for practical reasons.

faqs.q: Can a notary refuse for any reason at all?
faqs.a: No. A notary may not refuse on the basis of race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, or similar protected characteristics.

faqs.q: Why would a notary refuse to notarize my document?
faqs.a: Most commonly: a signer is missing, identification is expired or unacceptable, the document has blank spaces, a required witness is absent, or the notary doubts the signer is acting voluntarily.

faqs.q: Can a notary use a translator?
faqs.a: Generally no. A notary normally must be able to communicate directly with the signer to be satisfied they are acting willingly and understand what they are signing.

posts.title: Can a Notary Notarize for Family Members?
posts.metaTitle: Can a Notary Notarize for a Family Member? Florida Rules & Risks
posts.metaDesc: Florida law restricts notarizing for a spouse and close relatives, and prohibits notarizing where the notary has a financial interest. Here is the safe rule.
keywords: can a notary notarize for family
posts.excerpt: The safest answer is don't. Florida law restricts it, and the practical risk outweighs the convenience.

sections.html:
Florida law restricts a notary from notarizing the signature of a spouse, parent, or child. Beyond those named relationships, the broader and more important rule is that a notary may not notarize a transaction in which the notary has a financial interest or is a party — see Fla. Stat. §117.107.

A notarization performed in violation can be challenged, and the notary can face disciplinary action.

This is the trap that catches people. You may be technically outside the named-relative restriction and still prohibited, because you stand to benefit.

Examples: notarizing a deed that transfers property to you; notarizing a document in a transaction where you earn a commission; notarizing paperwork for a business you own an interest in.

This is why a notary who is also a licensed real estate agent must be careful about notarizing in transactions where they are the agent of record. Read §117.107 in full if that describes you.

Even where technically permitted, notarizing for a relative invites a challenge to the document. If the instrument ever matters — a deed, a power of attorney, an estate document — an interested party can attack it on the basis of the relationship.

Use a disinterested notary. They are inexpensive and easy to find; a contested deed is neither.

faqs.q: Can a notary notarize for a family member in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida restricts notarizing the signature of a spouse, parent, or child. More broadly, a notary may not notarize any transaction in which the notary has a financial interest or is a party, under Fla. Stat. 117.107.

faqs.q: Can a notary notarize for a friend?
faqs.a: There is no prohibition based on friendship, but the financial interest rule still applies. A notary may not notarize a transaction they stand to benefit from.

faqs.q: What happens if a notary notarizes for a prohibited relative?
faqs.a: The notarization can be challenged and the document's validity called into question, and the notary may face disciplinary action.

faqs.q: Can a notary who is also a real estate agent notarize their own deal?
faqs.a: This is exactly the financial interest problem addressed by Fla. Stat. 117.107. A notary who earns a commission on the transaction should not notarize it and should read that section in full.

posts.title: What Is an Apostille?
posts.metaTitle: What Is an Apostille? Florida Apostille Process Explained (2026)
posts.metaDesc: An apostille authenticates a document for use in another country. How the Florida process works, what it costs, and how it differs from notarization.
posts.excerpt: An apostille is not a notarization. It authenticates the notary — for use abroad.

sections.html:
An apostille is a certificate that authenticates the origin of a public document so it will be recognised in another country. It exists under the Hague Apostille Convention.

Critically, an apostille does not certify that the contents of the document are true. It certifies that the signature, seal, or stamp on the document — typically a notary's — is genuine.

For Florida documents, the sequence is generally:

  1. The document is notarized by a Florida notary, or is a certified copy issued by a Florida agency
  2. The document is submitted to the Florida Department of State for the apostille
  3. The apostille is attached and the document is returned

If the destination country is not a party to the Hague Convention, you need authentication and consular legalisation instead, which involves the destination country's embassy or consulate and takes longer.

• Defective notarization. If the notarial certificate is incomplete or the seal is illegible, the apostille will be rejected. This is the single most common failure.
  • Wrong document. Vital records generally need to be a certified copy from the issuing agency, not a photocopy notarized by a notary.
  • Wrong process. Confirm whether the destination country is a Hague member before starting.

Many mobile notaries offer apostille courier services — handling the notarization and the submission. That is a service fee, entirely separate from the $10 statutory cap on the notarial act.

faqs.q: What is an apostille?
faqs.a: An apostille is a certificate that authenticates the origin of a public document so it will be recognised in another country under the Hague Apostille Convention. It certifies that a signature or seal is genuine, not that the document's contents are true.

faqs.q: How do I get an apostille in Florida?
faqs.a: The document is generally notarized by a Florida notary or issued as a certified copy by a Florida agency, then submitted to the Florida Department of State, which attaches the apostille.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an apostille and notarization?
faqs.a: Notarization verifies the identity of the person signing. An apostille authenticates the notary's signature and seal so the document is recognised abroad. An apostille is applied after notarization, not instead of it.

faqs.q: What if the destination country is not part of the Hague Convention?
faqs.a: You need authentication and consular legalisation instead, which involves the destination country's embassy or consulate and generally takes longer.

posts.title: Hospital and Care Facility Notary Signings
posts.metaTitle: Hospital Notary Services: How to Get Documents Signed Bedside
posts.metaDesc: How bedside notarizations work, what to prepare, and how capacity and witness requirements are handled in hospitals and care facilities.
posts.excerpt: The most time-sensitive notary work there is, and the most likely to be refused if you're unprepared.

sections.html:
Hospitals and care facilities rarely have a notary on staff, and when they do, that notary usually cannot notarize for patients due to facility policy or conflict-of-interest rules.

These signings are typically powers of attorney, advance directives, healthcare surrogate designations, deeds, and estate documents — often on short notice.

• Witnesses. A Florida power of attorney needs two. Hospital staff frequently decline to serve. Arrange your own.
  • Identification for the patient. If ID is at home, say so when booking — credible witnesses may be needed and that changes who must attend.
  • The complete document, with no blanks.
  • Confirm visiting access and any facility restrictions.

This is where bedside signings most often stop. A notary must be satisfied the signer is acting willingly and appears aware of what they are doing.

A notary is not qualified to assess legal capacity and does not certify it. But a notary who has genuine doubt — heavy sedation, apparent confusion, or someone else answering for the patient — should decline, and a competent one will.

If capacity is genuinely in question, involve the attorney who drafted the document and the treating physician. Calling a second notary to get a different answer is not the solution.

faqs.q: Can a notary come to a hospital?
faqs.a: Yes. Mobile notaries routinely handle bedside signings at hospitals and care facilities, most often for powers of attorney, advance directives, healthcare surrogate designations, and estate documents.

faqs.q: Can hospital staff serve as witnesses?
faqs.a: Often they decline, due to facility policy or conflict-of-interest concerns. Arrange your own witnesses in advance — a Florida power of attorney requires two.

faqs.q: What if the patient has no ID at the hospital?
faqs.a: Tell the notary when booking. Florida permits identification through credible witnesses who personally know the signer, but they must attend and be identified themselves.

faqs.q: What if the patient is sedated or confused?
faqs.a: A notary must be satisfied the signer is acting willingly and appears aware of what they are signing. A notary with genuine doubt should decline. If capacity is in question, involve the drafting attorney and the treating physician.

posts.title: Jurat vs. Acknowledgment in Florida
posts.metaTitle: Jurat vs. Acknowledgment in Florida: How to Tell Which One a Document Needs
posts.metaDesc: An acknowledgment confirms a signature is genuine and voluntary. A jurat is a sworn oath that the contents are true. Choosing wrong invalidates the notarization — here is how to tell them apart.
posts.excerpt: Two acts, two certificates, two very different legal effects. Mixing them up is the most common reason a document comes back.

sections.html:
Florida notaries perform several distinct acts, but two account for nearly every notarization you will ever see. They look similar on the page and are constantly confused.

An acknowledgment is the signer telling the notary: that is my signature, and I made it freely. The signature does not have to be made in front of the notary. It can have been signed an hour earlier at the kitchen table — the signer simply appears and acknowledges it. Deeds, mortgages, and most real-property instruments take acknowledgments.

A jurat is the signer swearing: the contents of this document are true. A jurat requires two things an acknowledgment does not. The signer must sign in the notary's presence, and the notary must administer an oath or affirmation out loud. Affidavits, sworn statements, and verified pleadings take jurats.

The tell in the certificate wording: an acknowledgment reads “acknowledged before me”; a jurat reads “sworn to (or affirmed) and subscribed before me.” That word subscribed is the giveaway — it means signed in the notary's presence.

sections.h: Why the wrong one is a real problem
sections.html:
A notarial certificate is a sworn statement by the notary about what happened. If you complete a jurat, you are certifying under your commission that you administered an oath. If you did not actually administer one, the certificate is false — and Fla. Stat. §117.107(9) prohibits a notary from certifying to something that did not occur in the notary's presence.

Downstream, the consequences are practical. A court can refuse an affidavit that carries an acknowledgment instead of a jurat, because nothing was ever sworn. A recording office can reject a deed whose certificate does not track the statutory acknowledgment language. In a loan package, a mismatched certificate is one of the most common reasons documents are sent back for re-execution — which means a second appointment, at your cost.

sections.h: How to choose without giving legal advice
sections.html:
Here is the constraint that trips up new notaries: under Fla. Stat. §117.05, choosing the notarial act for the signer is legal advice, and a notary who is not a Florida attorney may not give it. But you also cannot notarize without knowing which act to perform. The way through:

  • Look for pre-printed certificate wording. Most documents already contain it. If the document says “sworn to and subscribed,” it is a jurat. Perform that act. You have not chosen anything — the drafter did.
  • If there is no wording, ask the signer. “Do you need to swear that this is true, or just confirm that this is your signature?” That is a factual question, not advice. The signer chooses; you perform.
  • If the signer does not know, stop. Refer them to the party who requested the document — the court, the lender, the agency. They will tell the signer which act is required in about thirty seconds.
  • Never guess, and never fill in blank certificate wording based on what you assume the document is for.

Whichever act you perform, §117.05(4) requires the certificate to state the venue, the type of act, whether the signer appeared physically or by audio-video link, the exact date, the signer's name, how you identified them, and your signature, printed name, and seal.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a jurat and an acknowledgment?
faqs.a: An acknowledgment confirms the signer's signature is genuine and voluntary; the signature may have been made before the notary appointment. A jurat is an oath that the contents of the document are true, and it requires the signer to sign in the notary's presence and to be sworn by the notary.

faqs.q: Can a notary decide which one my document needs?
faqs.a: No. Selecting the notarial act is legal advice, and a Florida notary who is not an attorney may not give it. The notary will follow the certificate wording already printed on the document, or ask you which act you need. If you do not know, ask the agency, court, or lender requesting the document.

faqs.q: Does a jurat require me to sign in front of the notary?
faqs.a: Yes. A jurat requires the signature to be made in the notary's presence and requires the notary to administer an oath or affirmation. An acknowledgment does not — the signer only has to appear and acknowledge that the signature is theirs.

faqs.q: What happens if the wrong certificate is used?
faqs.a: The notarization can be treated as defective. Courts can reject an affidavit that was never sworn, recording offices can reject an instrument whose certificate does not match statutory form, and lenders routinely send loan documents back for re-execution. For the notary it is also a compliance problem, since the certificate is a sworn statement about what actually occurred.

faqs.q: What does “subscribed” mean on a notarial certificate?
faqs.a: Subscribed means signed. On a Florida certificate, “sworn to (or affirmed) and subscribed before me” signals a jurat — the signer both swore an oath and signed while the notary watched.

posts.title: Does a Florida Notary Have to Keep a Journal?
posts.metaTitle: Florida Notary Journal Requirements: What the Law Actually Requires (and What It Doesn't)
posts.metaDesc: Florida does not require a paper journal for in-person notarizations — but it does require a 10-year electronic journal for remote online notarizations under §117.245. Here is the real rule, and why you should keep one anyway.
keywords: do notaries have to keep a journal
posts.excerpt: The law is narrower than most notaries assume — and your own protection is broader than the law.

sections.h: The short answer, split two ways
sections.html:
For traditional, in-person notarizations, Florida does not require a journal. Chapter 117 imposes no recordkeeping obligation on a notary performing paper notarizations. Florida is in the minority here; many states do require one.

For remote online notarization, Florida absolutely does. Fla. Stat. §117.245 requires every Florida online notary to keep an electronic journal of online notarizations, and to retain it — along with the audio-video recording of each session — for at least 10 years after the notarial act.

So the answer depends entirely on which chair you are sitting in. If you commission for RON, you have a statutory retention program to run. If you only stamp paper, you have none.

sections.h: What a RON journal has to contain
sections.html:
Under §117.245, each electronic journal entry must record:

  • The date and time of the notarization
  • The type of notarial act performed
  • A description of the record being notarized
  • The name and address of each principal
  • The evidence of identity relied on — including the credential analysis and identity proofing results
  • Any fee charged

Separately, the RON service provider must retain an uninterrupted and unedited audio-video recording of the entire session — the principal's appearance, the identity confirmation, the notary's recitation, the declaration that the signing is voluntary, and everything said and done throughout.

Both the journal and the recordings run on the same 10-year clock. Retention may be delegated to a secure repository, but the Department of State must be notified within 30 days with the repository's contact information. Notably, recordings tied to electronic wills follow the separate qualified-custodian rules in Florida's will statutes.

sections.h: Why keep a paper journal anyway
sections.html:
No statute requires it. Every experienced notary keeps one regardless, for one reason: a journal is the only evidence you will ever have that you did it right.

A signature is disputed two years after the fact. A deed is challenged. A borrower claims they were never shown a document. You will not remember that appointment. Your journal will — the date, the ID you inspected, the document, the fee, and the signer's own signature in your book.

What to record for each act: date and time, act type, document title and date, signer's name, how you identified them, the fee charged, and the signer's signature. Keep it bound, sequential, and never pre-signed. If a signer refuses to sign your journal, note it and proceed — nothing in Florida law makes their signature a condition of the notarization.

One caution, and it is a real one: a Florida notary's journal is your record, not a public record. Do not hand the whole book to anyone who asks. If someone needs a specific entry, produce that entry — not the personal information of every other signer in the book.

faqs.q: Is a notary journal required in Florida?
faqs.a: Not for traditional in-person notarizations — Chapter 117 does not require one. It is required for remote online notarization: Fla. Stat. §117.245 requires a Florida online notary to keep an electronic journal of every online notarization.

faqs.q: How long must a Florida RON notary keep records?
faqs.a: At least 10 years after the date of the notarial act, for both the electronic journal and the audio-video recording of the session. Retention can be delegated to a secure repository if the Department of State is notified within 30 days.

faqs.q: What has to be in a Florida electronic notary journal?
faqs.a: Under §117.245: the date and time, the type of notarial act, a description of the record, the name and address of each principal, the evidence of identity used, and any fee charged.

faqs.q: Should I keep a journal even though Florida doesn't require it?
faqs.a: Yes. A journal is the only contemporaneous evidence you will have if a notarization is ever challenged, and it costs a few dollars. Record the date, act type, document, signer, method of identification, fee, and have the signer sign the entry.

faqs.q: Is my notary journal a public record?
faqs.a: No. A Florida notary's journal is the notary's own business record, not a government public record. Produce specific entries when there is a legitimate need; do not hand over the entire book, which would expose other signers' information.

posts.title: How Much Do Loan Signing Agents Make in Florida?
posts.metaTitle: How Much Do Loan Signing Agents Make in Florida? Real Per-Signing Fees and Annual Math
posts.metaDesc: Loan signing fees in Florida generally run $75–$200 per appointment depending on who hires you and what the package is. Here is the honest math, including the costs nobody mentions.
keywords: how much do loan signing agents make
posts.excerpt: The per-signing number is easy to find. The number that matters is what is left after printing, driving, and unpaid drive time.

sections.html:
Loan signing fees in Florida are set by whoever hires you, and they cluster in fairly predictable bands:

  • $75–$100 — high-volume national signing services, simple refinances, e-docs, often a bidding platform where the fee is set before you see the file
  • $100–$150 — the working middle of the market. Standard purchase or refinance package, printed two sets, one signer table
  • $150–$250 — direct title and escrow work, reverse mortgages, HELOCs, split signings, out-of-area travel, and rush or after-hours appointments
  • $25 flat — the statutory maximum a Florida online notary may charge for the RON act itself under Fla. Stat. §117.275. Note carefully: that cap is on the notarial act, not on the signing-agent service fee, which is a separate business service

The single biggest determinant of your rate is not skill. It is who is on the other end of the phone. National signing services take a spread out of the middle; title companies and escrow offices that hire you directly do not. The same two-hour appointment can pay $85 or $175 based purely on that.

Take a working agent at $125 average per signing:

  • 2 signings a week — roughly $13,000 a year. This is a side income, and it is what most new agents actually do
  • 5 signings a week — roughly $32,500 a year
  • 10 signings a week — roughly $65,000 a year. This is a full-time practice with a real book of direct title relationships

Now subtract what nobody puts in the marketing material. Printing a two-set loan package runs $4–$12 in toner and paper. You will drive 20–40 miles round trip and burn 45 minutes each way that nobody pays for. Background screening runs $60–$100 a year, E&O insurance $50–$300 depending on limit, and a dual-tray laser printer is a $400–$900 capital outlay before your first job.

Realistically, expect 15–25% of gross to disappear into cost of goods, before self-employment tax. A $125 signing nets closer to $95–$105 in your pocket, for what is often two-and-a-half hours door to door.

Four things separate a $13,000 side income from a $65,000 practice, and none of them are a certification badge:

  • Direct relationships. Every dollar a signing service earns came out of the middle of your fee. Title companies, escrow officers, and real estate attorneys hire directly and pay 30–60% more for the same work.
  • Capacity to say yes. The agent who answers at 4:45 p.m. for a 7:00 p.m. signing gets called first forever after. Availability compounds.
  • Zero-error record. A single missed notarial certificate that forces a re-signing costs the title company more than your fee. Agents who never cause a rework get the good files.
  • RON capability. A Florida online notary can take signings outside driving distance, with no printing and no windshield time — changing the economics of the low-fee end of the market entirely.

faqs.q: How much does a loan signing agent make per signing in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically $75–$100 from high-volume national signing services, $100–$150 for standard work, and $150–$250 for direct title work, reverse mortgages, split signings, or rush appointments.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary charge more than $10 for a loan signing?
faqs.a: Yes. The $10 cap in Fla. Stat. §117.05 applies to each notarial act. A loan signing fee is payment for a separate business service — travel, printing, presenting and returning the package. The notarial fees within it remain subject to the statutory cap and should be identifiable.

faqs.q: Is being a loan signing agent full-time income in Florida?
faqs.a: It can be, but it requires roughly 10 signings a week and direct title relationships, which typically takes a year or more to build. At $125 average that is around $65,000 gross, less 15–25% in printing, mileage, insurance, and screening costs.

faqs.q: What are the hidden costs of loan signing work?
faqs.a: Printing a two-set package costs $4–$12, unpaid drive time runs 45 minutes each way, background screening is $60–$100 a year, E&O insurance is $50–$300 a year, and a dual-tray laser printer is a $400–$900 upfront purchase.

faqs.q: Do you get paid more working directly with title companies?
faqs.a: Generally yes — often 30–60% more for identical work, because no signing service is taking a spread out of the middle. Direct relationships are the main lever on a signing agent's income.

posts.title: Notary Signing Agent vs. Notary Public
posts.metaTitle: Notary Signing Agent vs. Notary Public: What's the Difference in Florida?
posts.metaDesc: A notary public is a state commission. A notary signing agent is a private specialization on top of it — no extra license, no extra authority, and very different pay.
keywords: notary signing agent vs notary public
what is a notary signing agent
posts.excerpt: One is a state commission. The other is a job description — and the state has nothing to do with it.

sections.html:
A notary public is commissioned by the Florida Department of State under Chapter 117. That commission is the entire source of your legal authority to administer oaths, take acknowledgments, and apply a seal. It runs four years and is regulated by the state.

A notary signing agent — also called a loan signing agent — is a notary public who has additionally learned to conduct mortgage loan closings. It is a private-market specialization. Florida does not license, register, or recognize “signing agent” as a separate status. There is no state exam, no state credential, and no state authority attached to it.

Everything that makes someone a signing agent comes from the private side: a background screening the lender's vendor management rules require, an E&O policy the title company wants to see, familiarity with the 40–150 documents in a loan package, and a printer that can handle legal-size paper.

sections.h: What the work looks like side by side
sections.html:
General notary workLoan signing
Typical fee$10 per act plus travel$75–$250 per appointment
Time on site10–20 minutes45–90 minutes
Documents1–340–150
EquipmentSeal and journalDual-tray laser printer, scanner, shipping
Who hires youThe publicTitle, escrow, signing services
Required by lawState commissionState commission only — the rest is private

The economics are the whole reason notaries move toward signing work. Ten general notary acts at $10 is $100 and ten separate trips. One loan signing is $125 and one trip.

sections.h: Certification: what it does and doesn't buy
sections.html:
Signing agent certifications sold by the National Notary Association, LSS, and others are private credentials. They are worth understanding honestly.

What they do: teach the documents, and satisfy the vendor-management checkbox many signing services and title companies use when they onboard you. Most of those companies require a current background screening and proof of E&O, and a recognized certification is the easiest way to satisfy their intake form.

What they do not do: grant any legal authority whatsoever. A certification does not expand what you may notarize, does not override the $10 statutory cap on the notarial act, and does not permit you to explain loan terms. A signing agent still may not give legal advice, and under Fla. Stat. §117.05 that includes explaining what a document means or advising a borrower on whether to sign it.

That last limit is the one that gets signing agents in trouble. You may point to where a term appears in the document and read it aloud. You may not interpret it. “That's your interest rate, on line 3 — and if that isn't what you expected, let's call your loan officer before you sign” is the whole script.

faqs.q: Is a notary signing agent the same as a notary public?
faqs.a: No. A notary public is a state commission that grants legal authority. A notary signing agent is a notary public who specializes in mortgage loan closings — a private-market specialization that Florida does not license or recognize as a separate status.

faqs.q: Do you need a special license to be a loan signing agent in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida requires only an active notary commission. Background screening, E&O insurance, and signing agent certification are private requirements imposed by title companies and signing services, not by the state.

faqs.q: Is signing agent certification worth it?
faqs.a: It teaches the loan documents and satisfies the onboarding requirements most signing services use, which makes it practically useful. It grants no legal authority and does not change what a notary may do under Chapter 117.

faqs.q: Can a loan signing agent explain the loan documents?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect is legal advice, which a Florida notary who is not an attorney may not give. A signing agent may identify where a term appears and read it aloud, then refer questions to the loan officer or closing agent.

faqs.q: Why do loan signings pay so much more than notary work?
faqs.a: Because the fee pays for the whole service — printing 40–150 pages twice, traveling, presenting the package, and shipping it back — not for the notarial acts, which remain capped at $10 each under Fla. Stat. §117.05.

posts.title: How to Get Loan Signing Jobs in Florida
posts.metaTitle: How to Get Loan Signing Jobs: Signing Services, Title Companies, and Direct Work
posts.metaDesc: There are exactly three channels for loan signing work in Florida, they pay very differently, and most new agents only ever find the worst one. Here is how to work all three.
keywords: how to get loan signing jobs
posts.excerpt: Three channels, in ascending order of what they pay and descending order of how easy they are to start.

sections.html:
Signing services are middlemen. A title company hands them a closing, they find a notary, and they keep the spread. They are the easiest channel to enter and the lowest paying — which is exactly why every new agent starts here.

The work: register a profile with as many as you can tolerate, keep your background screening and E&O current, and answer fast. Volume platforms dispatch to whoever confirms first. Most give you the fee before you see the file, and the fee is not really negotiable until you have a track record with that particular scheduler.
