Treat this channel as paid training. You learn the documents on someone else's file, you build a screening and insurance history, and you find out whether you actually like the work — all without having to sell anything. Then you start migrating up.

sections.h: Channel two: title and escrow direct
sections.html:
This is where the money is. A title company that calls you directly pays what the signing service was charging them, not what the signing service was paying you — typically 30–60% more for the identical appointment.

How it actually works, and it is unglamorous:

  • Build a list of local title and escrow offices in your county and the two adjacent ones. Independent shops respond far better than national operations, which route everything through vendor management.
  • Ask for the closing coordinator or post-closer, not the owner and not “whoever handles notaries.” The coordinator is the person whose day gets ruined when a signing falls through.
  • Lead with availability, not credentials. They do not care about your certification. They care whether you can cover a 6 p.m. signing in Sanford on Thursday. “I cover Seminole, Orange, and Volusia, I have a dual-tray printer, and I can take same-day” is the entire pitch.
  • Send one page, then follow up once. Name, counties covered, commission number and expiration, RON capability, screening date, E&O limit, phone. That is the whole document.
  • Get on the backup list. Nobody replaces a working notary on day one. You get in when their regular is sick, and then you never leave.

The slowest to build and the only one nobody can take away from you. Two pieces:

Be findable. A Google Business Profile with your service area, real hours, and actual reviews will out-produce every directory listing you pay for. Beyond that, list where title companies and the public actually look — including free public registers like this one, which is why it exists.

Be adjacent to closings. Real estate agents, mortgage brokers, estate planning attorneys, and elder-law practices all generate notarizations continuously and all have someone they currently call. Being the person they call instead is a relationship question, not a marketing question.

One honest caution on outreach: cold text messages to phone numbers you scraped are a TCPA problem, not a growth channel, and the statutory damages run $500–$1,500 per message. Email and phone calls to businesses are fine. Bulk SMS to individuals is not.

faqs.q: How do I get my first loan signing job?
faqs.a: Register with signing services. They are the lowest-paying channel but the only one that will hire an agent with no track record. Keep a current background screening and E&O policy, and confirm assignments fast — most volume platforms dispatch to whoever answers first.

faqs.q: How do I get title companies to hire me directly?
faqs.a: Build a list of local title and escrow offices, ask for the closing coordinator or post-closer, and lead with coverage area and availability rather than credentials. Ask to be added to their backup list — that is how nearly every direct relationship actually starts.

faqs.q: How much more do direct title clients pay?
faqs.a: Usually 30–60% more for the same appointment, because no signing service is taking a spread. A signing that pays $95 through a service commonly pays $135–$150 direct.

faqs.q: Do I need a website to get signing work?
faqs.a: No. A Google Business Profile, listings in notary registers, and direct relationships with local title offices produce more work than a website for most agents. A site helps with inbound public work over time.

faqs.q: Can I text local notary prospects or title companies to get work?
faqs.a: Do not send bulk SMS to numbers you collected without consent — the TCPA carries statutory damages of $500–$1,500 per message. Phone calls and email to business contacts are the safe channels.

posts.title: What Is a Signing Service?
posts.metaTitle: What Is a Signing Service? How Notary Dispatch Actually Works in a Real Estate Closing
posts.metaDesc: A signing service sits between the title company and the notary, schedules the appointment, and keeps part of the fee. Here is what they do, what they charge, and when to work around them.
posts.excerpt: The layer between the title company and the notary — what it does, and what it costs both sides.

sections.html:
When a mortgage closes, someone has to physically get the documents in front of the borrower, watch them sign in the right places, notarize what needs notarizing, and get the package back to the closer before funding. Title companies could staff that themselves. Most do not, because closings happen at 7 p.m. across three counties and the volume is unpredictable.

A signing service takes that problem. Given a closing, it finds a qualified notary in the borrower's area, confirms the appointment, sends the documents, tracks the scan-back and the shipping, and takes responsibility for the package arriving. It is a dispatch and quality-control layer.

The chain is: lender → title/escrow → signing service → notary signing agent → borrower. Sometimes the signing service is skipped and title calls the notary directly. Sometimes a title company runs its own in-house signing service. The function is the same either way.

sections.h: What they charge and what they pay
sections.html:
A signing service typically bills the title company $150–$250 for a standard signing and pays the notary $75–$125. The spread — often 40–50% — is the business.

That spread is not pure margin. The service is carrying real costs: vendor management and credential verification, 24/7 scheduling staff, e-signing and tracking software, errors-and-omissions coverage layered above the notary's, and the liability if a package is late or wrong. For a title company processing dozens of closings a month, outsourcing that is usually cheaper than staffing it.

For the notary, the tradeoff is simpler: the service brings you work you did not have to sell, and charges you roughly half the fee for it. Early on that is a good deal. Once you can generate your own work, it stops being one.

sections.h: What this means for each side
sections.html:
If you are a notary: work with signing services to learn and to fill your calendar, but understand the fee ceiling is structural. No amount of good work changes a spread-based business model. Move a portion of your book direct over time — not all of it, because signing services smooth out the gaps that direct clients leave.

If you are a title company or closer: the value is dispatch reliability and coverage, especially for after-hours and out-of-area signings. What you give up is a direct line to the person actually sitting with your borrower. Many closers run a hybrid — a short direct bench of known notaries for their core counties, a signing service for everything outside it.

A note on directories: a notary directory is not a signing service, and the distinction matters. A directory lists notaries and lets people find them; it does not dispatch, does not carry the package liability, and does not take a spread on the fee. If a platform is charging you for placement, it is a directory. If it is scheduling you and paying you, it is a signing service.

faqs.q: What does a signing service do?
faqs.a: It sits between the title company and the notary: it finds a qualified signing agent in the borrower's area, schedules and confirms the appointment, delivers the documents, tracks the scan-back and shipping, and takes responsibility for the completed package.

faqs.q: How much do signing services pay notaries?
faqs.a: Typically $75–$125 per standard signing, against $150–$250 billed to the title company. The 40–50% spread covers scheduling staff, vendor management, software, insurance, and the service's own liability.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a signing service and a title company?
faqs.a: The title company handles the closing itself — title search, escrow, funding, recording. The signing service only handles getting the documents signed and notarized, and only when the title company chooses to outsource it.

faqs.q: Should notaries work with signing services or go direct?
faqs.a: Both. Signing services provide volume with no sales effort and fill calendar gaps, but the fee ceiling is structural. Direct title relationships pay 30–60% more. Most established agents keep a mix.

faqs.q: Is a notary directory the same as a signing service?
faqs.a: No. A directory lists notaries so they can be found; it does not dispatch work, hold package liability, or take a cut of the signing fee. A signing service schedules the appointment and pays the notary.

posts.title: How Title Companies Choose Notaries
posts.metaTitle: How Title Companies Choose Notaries: What Closers Actually Check Before They Call You
posts.metaDesc: Closers are not evaluating your credentials — they are managing risk and a clock. Here is what a title company verifies, in what order, and what gets a notary quietly dropped.
posts.excerpt: Written for closers and post-closers — and for notaries who want to understand what is actually being evaluated.

sections.h: What gets verified before you're on the list
sections.html:
Before a title company sends a borrower's loan package to a stranger, someone confirms four things. In practice, in this order:

  • Active commission. Name, commission number, and expiration verified against the Florida Department of State record. This is non-negotiable and it is the first thing checked — a notarization performed on an expired commission can cloud title.
  • Background screening. Most lenders' vendor-management policies require a recent screening, and many require it refreshed annually. The requirement flows from the lender to the title company to you.
  • E&O insurance. A certificate of coverage, usually $25,000 minimum and often $100,000 for loan signing work. Larger operations may require being named as an additional interest.
  • Coverage and capacity. Which counties, how far, evenings, weekends, same-day. This is what determines whether you get called often once you are approved.

Notably absent from that list: certifications, years of experience, and anything on a website. Those come up almost never.

sections.h: What actually gets a notary called again
sections.html:
Approval is a checklist. Repeat business is behavioral, and closers are remarkably consistent about what they value:

  • The package comes back clean the first time. A missed initial, a blank notarial certificate, a wrong date — any of these means a re-signing, an angry borrower, and a funding delay. Rework costs the title company more than the entire notary fee.
  • You answer the phone. Coordinators are working against a funding deadline. The notary who confirms in ten minutes beats the notary with a better resume who confirms tomorrow.
  • You scan back the same night. Not the next morning. Funding often waits on it.
  • You call when something is wrong rather than improvising. A borrower whose ID is expired, a name that does not match, a missing spouse — the closer wants to hear about it from the table, not discover it in review.
  • You stay in your lane. A notary who explains loan terms to a borrower creates real liability for the title company. One incident ends the relationship.

sections.h: If you're the title company: how to build a bench
sections.html:
Most closers we talk to run a hybrid model — a small direct bench for core counties, a signing service for everything else. Building the bench:

  • Recruit by county, not by volume. Two or three reliable notaries per county you close in is plenty. Density beats breadth.
  • Verify commissions against the state record, not the notary's own claim — and re-verify on a schedule, since commissions expire on a rolling four-year cycle.
  • Add RON capability deliberately. A Florida online notary can close a borrower who is out of state or in another country. The RON act itself is capped at $25 under Fla. Stat. §117.275, and there is no printing or driving — which makes it materially cheaper for the files where it works.
  • Give feedback once. Most notary errors are fixable, and an agent who is told exactly what went wrong usually never repeats it.

State Notary Agent maintains a free, searchable register of Florida notaries drawn from the Department of State's own published journals, including commission numbers and expiration dates — which is the fastest way to verify a notary you are considering.

faqs.q: What do title companies require from a notary?
faqs.a: An active Florida commission verified against the Department of State record, a recent background screening, E&O insurance (commonly $25,000 minimum and often $100,000 for loan signings), and clearly stated county coverage and availability.

faqs.q: How much E&O insurance do title companies require?
faqs.a: Most require at least $25,000, and many require $100,000 for loan signing work. Some larger operations ask to be named as an additional interest on the policy.

faqs.q: Why do title companies stop using a notary?
faqs.a: Most often for packages that come back needing rework — blank or wrong notarial certificates, missed signatures, wrong dates — or for slow confirmation and late scan-backs. Explaining loan terms to a borrower ends the relationship immediately.

faqs.q: How do I verify a Florida notary's commission?
faqs.a: Check the name, commission number, and expiration against the Florida Department of State's notary records. State Notary Agent's free register is built from the Department's own published journals and shows commission numbers and expiration dates.

faqs.q: Should a title company use a signing service or hire notaries directly?
faqs.a: Most use both: a small direct bench of two or three verified notaries in each core county, and a signing service for after-hours, out-of-area, and overflow. Direct is cheaper per signing; the service provides coverage and dispatch reliability.

posts.title: Notary Errors That Delay Closings
posts.metaTitle: The 10 Notary Errors That Delay Real Estate Closings (and How to Prevent Them)
posts.metaDesc: Nearly every rework in a loan package traces back to the same short list of notarial mistakes. Here they are, ranked by how often they force a re-signing.
posts.excerpt: A re-signing costs the title company more than the notary fee. Here is the list that causes almost all of them.

sections.h: The errors that force a re-signing
sections.html:
1. Blank or incomplete notarial certificate. The single most common defect. A missing venue, an unfilled date, an omitted signer name — Fla. Stat. §117.05(4) requires the venue, the act type, whether the signer appeared physically or by audio-video, the exact date, the signer's name, the identification method, and the notary's signature, printed name, and seal. Any one missing is a defective notarization.
  2. Wrong certificate type. An acknowledgment completed where the document called for a jurat, or the reverse. The jurat requires an oath actually administered and the signature made in the notary's presence.
  3. Date mismatch. The notarial date must be the date the signer appeared. Backdating to a lender's requested date is a serious violation, not a courtesy.
  4. Seal illegible or overlapping text. §117.05(3)(a) requires photographically reproducible black ink. A seal stamped over printed text can render a recorded instrument unacceptable.
  5. Name variance. The signature, the printed name, the ID, and the vesting on the deed all have to reconcile. “Robert J. Smith” signing a deed vested in “Robert James Smith” needs to be addressed at the table, not in post-closing.

1. Missing witnesses on a deed. Fla. Stat. §689.01 requires two subscribing witnesses for a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property. The notary may serve as one only if the notary actually observed the signing — and even then, a second witness is still required. Mortgages are treated differently; see §697.02 and §695.26(1)(f).
  2. Notarizing outside the signer's presence. A spouse who “will sign later,” a document dropped off already signed for a jurat, a signer in the next room. §117.107(9) prohibits certifying to an act that did not occur in the notary's presence.
  3. Unacceptable identification. Expired ID, no ID with reliance on a document the statute does not authorize, or accepting a photocopy. Identification must satisfy §117.05(5).
  4. Missed signature or initial pages. Not a notarial defect, but the most common practical cause of a package coming back. It is why closers check page counts before releasing funds.
  5. Explaining the loan. A notary who answers “what does this mean” creates unauthorized-practice exposure for everyone in the chain — and it is prohibited under §117.05 for a non-attorney notary.

Almost all of the above disappear with a fixed sequence at the table:

  • Before you leave the house: confirm the signer's legal name against the documents, and confirm the number of witnesses the package requires. Bring a second witness if a deed is in the stack and none is arranged.
  • Before anything is signed: inspect the ID, confirm it is unexpired, and confirm the name reconciles. Raise variances now, not at page 60.
  • At each notarial certificate: fill it completely before you stamp. A stamped page with a blank line will be caught in review; a completed one will not.
  • Before you leave the table: page through the entire package once for signatures, initials, and dates. Two minutes here saves a re-signing.
  • Same night: scan back. Funding frequently waits on it.

If something is wrong and cannot be cured at the table — an expired ID, an absent spouse, a signer who does not appear to understand what they are signing — call the closer from the driveway. A rescheduled signing is a minor annoyance. A defective one is a title problem.

faqs.q: What is the most common notary error in a loan package?
faqs.a: An incomplete notarial certificate — a blank venue, date, or signer name. Fla. Stat. §117.05(4) requires the venue, act type, method of appearance, exact date, signer's name, identification method, and the notary's signature, printed name, and seal.

faqs.q: Can a notary backdate a notarization if the lender asks?
faqs.a: No. The notarial date must be the date the signer actually appeared. Backdating is a serious violation of a Florida notary's duties and can expose the notary to suspension of the commission and personal liability.

faqs.q: Does a Florida deed need witnesses in addition to a notary?
faqs.a: Yes. Fla. Stat. §689.01 requires two subscribing witnesses for a conveyance of an interest in Florida real property. A notary may serve as one witness only if the notary actually observed the signing, and a second witness is still required.

faqs.q: What happens if a notary certificate is filled out wrong?
faqs.a: The notarization is defective. In a loan package that usually means a re-signing, which delays funding and costs the title company more than the entire notary fee. On a recorded instrument it can create a title defect.

faqs.q: Can a notary explain what a loan document says?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect is legal advice, which a Florida notary who is not an attorney may not give. The notary may identify where a term appears and read it aloud, then refer the borrower to the loan officer or closing agent.

posts.title: IPEN vs. RON in Florida
posts.metaTitle: IPEN vs. RON in Florida: Electronic Notarization Explained (§117.021 and §117.225)
posts.metaDesc: Both are electronic notarizations, but only one lets the signer be somewhere else. IPEN is electronic-and-in-person; RON is electronic-and-remote, with a separate commission, bond, and fee cap.
posts.excerpt: The difference is not the documents. It is whether the signer is in the room.

sections.html:
IPEN — in-person electronic notarization. The signer is physically in front of the notary, as always. What changes is the medium: the document is electronic, the signature is electronic, and the notary applies an electronic signature and seal. Florida has authorized this for years under Fla. Stat. §117.021, which provides that a notary may perform an electronic notarization and that the electronic signature and seal are attached to or logically associated with the record.

RON — remote online notarization. The signer is not physically present. Appearance happens over live two-way audio-video, with identity established through credential analysis and knowledge-based identity proofing, and the whole session recorded. This is governed by §117.225 and the surrounding sections.

Put simply: IPEN changes the paper. RON changes the presence. That distinction drives every other difference between them.

IPENRON
Signer locationPhysically presentAnywhere, by audio-video
Extra commissionNo — standard commissionYes — separate online notary registration
Bond$7,500 (§117.01)Additional $25,000 (§117.225)
E&O requiredNot by statute$25,000 minimum (§117.225)
Fee cap$10 per act (§117.05)$25 per act (§117.275)
Recording & journalNot requiredElectronic journal + AV recording, 10 years (§117.245)
PlatformAny compliant e-sign systemRegistered RON service provider

sections.h: Which one a signing actually needs
sections.html:
IPEN fits a signer who is local but the file is fully digital — an e-closing at a title office, a hybrid package where some documents are wet-signed and the rest are electronic, or any situation where the county recorder accepts electronic recording and nobody wants to print 140 pages.

RON fits a signer who cannot physically be there: out of state, deployed, traveling, a seller who has already moved, an investor closing three properties in a week. It is also the answer for a rural signing where the drive is longer than the appointment.

Two practical constraints worth knowing before you promise either to a client:

  • Lender and title acceptance is not universal. Florida law permitting an act does not mean the lender's investor guidelines or the county recorder accept it for that particular instrument. Confirm before the appointment, not at it.
  • The fee caps apply to the notarial act only. The $10 and $25 caps in §117.05 and §117.275 govern the act. A signing agent's service fee — for conducting the closing, coordinating, and handling the package — is a separate charge and should be itemized as such.

faqs.q: What is the difference between IPEN and RON?
faqs.a: IPEN is in-person electronic notarization — the signer is physically present but the document, signature, and seal are electronic. RON is remote online notarization — the signer appears by live two-way audio-video from anywhere, with credential analysis, identity proofing, and a recorded session.

faqs.q: Does a Florida notary need a separate commission for IPEN?
faqs.a: No. A standard Florida notary commission covers in-person electronic notarization under Fla. Stat. §117.021. RON requires a separate registration as an online notary public, plus an additional $25,000 bond and $25,000 in E&O coverage under §117.225.

faqs.q: How much can a Florida notary charge for a remote online notarization?
faqs.a: Up to $25 per notarial act under Fla. Stat. §117.275, compared with the $10 cap for traditional acts under §117.05. Both caps apply to the notarial act itself, not to a separate signing-agent service fee.

faqs.q: Does IPEN require a recording or a journal?
faqs.a: No. The 10-year electronic journal and audio-video recording requirements in §117.245 apply to remote online notarization. IPEN carries no statutory recording or journal obligation.

faqs.q: Will lenders and county recorders accept IPEN and RON?
faqs.a: Not universally. Florida law authorizing an act is separate from whether a particular lender's investor guidelines or a particular county recorder will accept it for a given instrument. Confirm acceptance before scheduling the signing.

posts.title: Mobile Notary Travel Fees in Florida
posts.metaTitle: Mobile Notary Travel Fees in Florida: What You Can Legally Charge Above the $10 Cap
posts.metaDesc: The $10 statutory cap applies to the notarial act — not to travel. Here is how mobile notaries charge for travel lawfully, and the disclosure that keeps it clean.
keywords: how much can a mobile notary charge florida
posts.excerpt: One number is set by statute. The other is set by you — as long as you disclose it correctly.

sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §117.05(2)(a) is unambiguous: “The fee of a notary public may not exceed $10 for any one notarial act under this part.” That cap is on the notarial act — the acknowledgment, the jurat, the oath.

Driving to a hospital room in Kissimmee at 9 p.m. is not a notarial act. It is a separate service, and a mobile notary may charge for it. This is how every mobile notary practice in Florida operates, and it is why a $10 statutory fee and a $75 appointment are both true at the same time.

The rule that makes it work is separation and disclosure. The travel fee must be quoted and agreed in advance, and it must be presented as what it is — a travel or convenience charge, not a fee for the notarization. A client should be able to see the two numbers separately and understand which one the state caps.

Florida does not set a travel fee schedule, so the market does. Typical structures:

  • Flat travel fee by radius — $35–55 within 15 miles, $55–85 out to 30, $85–125 beyond. Simple to quote over the phone, which is most of the battle.
  • Base plus mileage — a $30–40 base plus $0.70–$1.00 per mile beyond a set radius. More defensible on long trips, harder to quote fast.
  • Premium surcharges — after-hours and weekend $20–40, same-day or emergency $25–50, hospital and correctional facilities $25–75 for the wait and access time, which is real.
  • Loan signings — priced as a single all-in service fee, $75–$250, covering travel, printing, presenting, and shipping the package.

An honest note on the low end: a general notary work call at $10 per act plus $40 travel is roughly $50–$70 for 90 minutes door to door. That is not a business by itself. It is why mobile notaries who make real money route toward loan signings, estate packages with a dozen acts, and facility work — where the act count or the fee per stop justifies the trip.

sections.h: How to quote it so it never becomes a problem
sections.html:
A clean quote sounds like this: “The notarization itself is $10 per signature — that's set by state law. My travel fee to come to you in Sanford is $45. So for two documents you're looking at $65 total. I'll text you that in writing before I head out.”

Four things that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Quote before you travel, every time. A fee introduced after arrival is the complaint that ends up at the Department of State.
  • Itemize on the receipt. Notarial acts on one line, travel on another. Never a single blended number with no explanation.
  • Say out loud that travel is not set by law. The client should never be able to say they thought the state required it.
  • Never charge above $10 per act, no matter what you call it. Relabeling part of the notarial fee as “processing” does not survive scrutiny.

One special case: solemnizing a marriage is governed by §117.045, under which a notary's fee may not exceed what circuit court clerks may charge for like services — a different rule from the §117.05 cap.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary charge more than $10?
faqs.a: Not for the notarial act — Fla. Stat. §117.05(2)(a) caps that at $10. A mobile notary may charge a separate travel or convenience fee, which is not a notarial fee, provided it is agreed in advance and itemized separately.

faqs.q: How much do mobile notaries charge for travel in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida sets no travel fee schedule. Common rates are $35–$55 within 15 miles, $55–$85 out to 30 miles, and more beyond, plus surcharges for after-hours, same-day, and hospital or correctional facility visits.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose the travel fee in advance?
faqs.a: Yes, as a matter of practice and of protecting yourself. Quote both the notarial fee and the travel fee before traveling, state clearly that the travel fee is not set by state law, and itemize the two separately on the receipt.

faqs.q: Can I charge a single flat fee that includes the notarization?
faqs.a: It is far safer not to. Blending them makes it impossible to show that the notarial act was charged at or below $10. Quote and itemize the notarial acts and the travel separately, even when you give the client a single total.

faqs.q: What can a Florida notary charge to perform a marriage?
faqs.a: Fla. Stat. §117.045 provides that a notary's fee for solemnizing a marriage may not exceed the fee that circuit court clerks may charge for like services — a separate rule from the $10 per-act cap in §117.05.

posts.title: How to Market a Mobile Notary Business
posts.metaTitle: How to Market a Mobile Notary Business in Florida: What Actually Produces Calls
posts.metaDesc: Most notary marketing advice sells you something. This is the honest ranking of what generates appointments, starting with the free thing almost everyone skips.
keywords: how to market a mobile notary business
posts.excerpt: Ranked by calls produced per dollar and hour spent — not by what is easiest to sell you.

sections.h: The things that actually work, in order
sections.html:
1. Google Business Profile. Free, and it out-produces everything else combined for public-facing notary work. Someone searching “notary near me” at 4 p.m. is calling one of the top three map results. Set a real service area, real hours — including the evening and weekend availability that differentiates you — and ask every single satisfied client for a review. Ten honest reviews will beat a $500 directory package.
  2. Local title and escrow offices. Not a marketing channel so much as a sales one, and the highest-value work available. Call, ask for the closing coordinator, offer coverage. See our guide on getting loan signing jobs.
  3. Adjacent professionals. Estate planning attorneys, elder law practices, real estate agents, mortgage brokers, assisted living facilities, hospitals, and structured settlement firms all generate repeat notarizations. Each already has someone they call. Being the second name on that list is enough to start.
  4. Directory listings. Useful and cheap, but not a substitute for the above. Be listed everywhere free — including public registers like this one — and be skeptical of paid placement until you can measure what a listing actually returned.
  5. A simple website. One page: counties covered, services, hours, phone, and your commission details. It converts the traffic the first three items generate. It does not generate traffic on its own for a while.

Bulk text messaging. Do not do it. Cold SMS to numbers you scraped or bought is a TCPA violation carrying statutory damages of $500–$1,500 per message, and Florida's own FTSA adds state exposure on top. There is no version of this that is worth it.

Paid ads before you have a conversion path. Google Ads for “mobile notary” can be genuinely expensive per click in Florida metros. Without reviews, a real profile, and a phone you answer, you will pay for clicks that go nowhere.

Expensive certifications as marketing. Certifications teach you the documents and satisfy signing service onboarding. They do not generate calls. No borrower has ever chosen a notary by credential.

Competing on price. The statutory act fee is fixed at $10, so the only thing left to discount is your travel — the part that actually costs you fuel and an hour of your life. Compete on availability and reliability instead. The notary who answers at 4:45 p.m. wins the job at any price.

• Week 1 — Claim and fully complete the Google Business Profile. Set service area and evening hours. List free in every notary register you can find. Order business cards.
  • Week 2 — Build a list of every title and escrow office within 30 miles. Call ten a day, ask for the closing coordinator, ask to be on the backup list. Register with five signing services.
  • Week 3 — Visit five adjacent businesses in person: an estate planning attorney, an assisted living facility, a real estate brokerage, a mortgage broker, a tax preparer. Leave a card and your counties.
  • Week 4 — Ask every client so far for a Google review. Follow up once with every title office that did not answer. Add RON capability if you have not — it removes your geographic ceiling entirely.

The thing that compounds is none of the above individually. It is that a notary who has been reachable, on time, and error-free for six months stops marketing, because the phone rings on its own.

faqs.q: What is the best way to get mobile notary clients?
faqs.a: A fully completed Google Business Profile with real hours and genuine reviews produces the most public-facing work, and direct outreach to local title and escrow offices produces the highest-paying work. Those two channels outperform everything else.

faqs.q: Do notary directory listings actually generate work?
faqs.a: Free listings are worth doing everywhere. Paid placement varies widely — list free first, track where calls actually come from, and only pay for placement you can show produced work.

faqs.q: Should mobile notaries run Google Ads?
faqs.a: Not until you have a Google Business Profile with reviews and a phone you reliably answer. Clicks are expensive in Florida metros and convert poorly without those in place.

faqs.q: Can I text or email prospects to market my notary business?
faqs.a: Email and phone calls to businesses are fine. Bulk SMS to individuals whose numbers you scraped or purchased violates the TCPA, with statutory damages of $500–$1,500 per message, plus Florida FTSA exposure.

faqs.q: Should I lower my prices to compete?
faqs.a: No. The notarial act fee is capped at $10 by statute, so discounting only cuts into your travel fee — the part that covers your actual costs. Compete on availability, response speed, and reliability instead.

posts.title: Florida Notary Seal Requirements
posts.metaTitle: Florida Notary Seal Requirements: What §117.05(3) Requires on Your Stamp
posts.metaDesc: Your seal must carry four specific elements and be stamped in photographically reproducible black ink. Get it wrong and recorded documents can be rejected.
posts.excerpt: Four required elements, one required ink color, and one rule about where not to put it.

sections.h: What the statute requires on the seal
sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §117.05(3)(a) sets out what a Florida notary's rubber stamp seal must contain:

  • The words “Notary Public-State of Florida”
  • The name of the notary public
  • The date of expiration of the commission
  • The commission number

The statute also specifies the medium: the rubber stamp seal must be affixed to the notarized paper document in photographically reproducible black ink. That requirement exists because recorded instruments are microfilmed and scanned — blue, purple, or light gray ink can vanish in reproduction, and a county recorder can refuse an instrument whose seal does not reproduce.

Your name on the seal must match the name on your commission exactly. If your commission reads “Robert J. Smith,” the seal reads “Robert J. Smith” — not “Bob Smith.”

sections.h: Practical rules that keep documents accepted
sections.html:
• Never stamp over printed text or a signature. If the seal obscures text, the recorder can reject the instrument. Find white space near the certificate. If there is none, that is a document-design problem to raise with the closer, not something to improvise around.
  • Never lend your seal. Your seal is your commission. An employer has no right to it, and a notarization made with your seal is your legal responsibility regardless of who pressed it.
  • Order a new seal at each renewal. Your commission number and expiration date change. A seal showing an expired date is a defective notarization even if your commission is current.
  • Keep it under your control. Locked drawer, not the shared supply cabinet. If a seal is lost or stolen, notify the Department of State and your bonding agency in writing.
  • Embossers are supplemental, not sufficient. A raised embossed seal alone does not reproduce photographically. Use the ink stamp; add the embosser only in addition if you want to.

sections.h: The seal is not the notarization
sections.html:
New notaries treat the stamp as the act. It is not. The seal is one required element of a notarial certificate that also has to state the venue, the type of notarial act, whether the signer appeared physically or by audio-video, the exact date, the signer's name, the method of identification, and the notary's signature and printed name — all under §117.05(4).

A perfectly stamped page with a blank certificate is a defective notarization. A completed certificate with a slightly crooked seal is a good one. Fill the certificate first, stamp last, and check it before you close the folder.

For online notarizations, the electronic signature and seal are governed separately — they must be attached to or logically associated with the electronic record, and RON acts carry the additional journal and recording requirements in §117.245.

faqs.q: What must a Florida notary seal include?
faqs.a: Under Fla. Stat. §117.05(3)(a): the words “Notary Public-State of Florida,” the notary's name, the commission expiration date, and the commission number. It must be affixed in photographically reproducible black ink.

faqs.q: What color ink must a Florida notary stamp use?
faqs.a: Photographically reproducible black ink. Blue, purple, or light-colored ink can fail to reproduce when an instrument is scanned or microfilmed, and a county recorder can reject the document.

faqs.q: Can a notary stamp over text on a document?
faqs.a: It should be avoided. A seal that obscures printed text or a signature can cause a recorded instrument to be rejected. Place the seal in clear space near the notarial certificate.

faqs.q: Do I need a new seal when I renew my commission?
faqs.a: Yes. Your commission number and expiration date change at renewal, and both appear on the seal. Using an old seal showing an expired date creates a defective notarization.

faqs.q: Is an embossed seal enough in Florida?
faqs.a: No. An embossed raised seal does not reproduce photographically. Florida requires the rubber stamp seal in reproducible black ink; an embosser may be used in addition but not instead.

posts.title: Acceptable ID for a Florida Notarization
posts.metaTitle: Acceptable ID for a Florida Notarization: The Full §117.05(5) List
posts.metaDesc: Florida law lists exactly which identification a notary may accept — and what to do when a signer has none of it. Here is the complete list and the credible witness alternative.
keywords: what id do i need for a notary florida
posts.excerpt: The statute is a closed list. If your ID is not on it, the notary is not being difficult.

sections.h: How a Florida notary may establish identity
sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §117.05(5) gives a notary exactly three routes to identify a signer, and no others:

  • Personal knowledge. The statute defines this narrowly: an acquaintance derived from association with the individual that establishes identity with at least reasonable certainty. Having met someone once is not personal knowledge.
  • An acceptable identification document from the statutory list below.
  • Credible witnesses — the fallback when the signer genuinely cannot produce ID.

There is no fourth option. A notary who identifies a signer some other way has performed a defective notarization, no matter how certain they were.

Under §117.05(5), the identification must be current or issued within the last five years, and must contain a photograph and signature. Acceptable documents include:

  • A Florida driver license or Florida identification card
  • A driver license or identification card issued by another U.S. state
  • A United States passport
  • A foreign passport stamped by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
  • A United States military or armed forces identification card
  • A veteran health identification card issued by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
  • An inmate identification card issued by the Florida Department of Corrections, for an inmate in custody
  • An identification card issued by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
  • For a confined inmate, a sworn certification from the officer having custody

What is not on the list, and gets turned away constantly: expired licenses, Social Security cards, birth certificates, credit cards, employee badges, student IDs, library cards, photographs of an ID on a phone, and photocopies. A birth certificate proves a birth, not that the person holding it is the person named.

sections.h: When the signer has no ID at all
sections.html:
The credible witness route in §117.05(5) exists for the person in a hospital bed whose wallet is at home, or the elderly signer whose license lapsed years ago. It is real, and it is more demanding than most people expect.

Either one credible witness personally known to the notary, or two credible witnesses who themselves present acceptable identification, must each swear in writing that:

  • The person signing is the person named in the document
  • That person is personally known to the witness
  • It would be very difficult or impossible for that person to obtain another acceptable form of identification
  • That person does not possess any of the statutory identification documents
  • The witness has no financial interest in and is not a party to the underlying transaction

That last condition is the one that fails in practice. The adult child arranging a parent's deed is a party in interest and cannot be the credible witness. Bring a neighbor.

faqs.q: What ID do I need for a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: A current Florida driver license or ID card, another state's license or ID, a U.S. passport, a USCIS-stamped foreign passport, a U.S. military or armed forces ID, a VA veteran health ID, a USCIS-issued ID card, or — for an inmate — a Florida Department of Corrections ID. It must carry a photograph and signature.

faqs.q: Can a notary accept an expired ID in Florida?
faqs.a: Only within the statutory window — the identification must be current or have been issued within the last five years. An older expired document is not acceptable evidence of identity.

faqs.q: Will a notary accept a birth certificate or Social Security card?
faqs.a: No. Neither is on the §117.05(5) list, and neither carries a photograph. They prove a fact about a person; they do not prove that the person presenting them is that person.

faqs.q: What if I have no ID at all?
faqs.a: Florida allows credible witnesses: either one witness personally known to the notary, or two witnesses who present acceptable ID. Each must swear in writing that they personally know you, that obtaining ID would be very difficult or impossible for you, and that they have no financial interest in the transaction.

faqs.q: Can a notary use a photo of my ID on my phone?
faqs.a: No. For an in-person notarization the notary must be presented with the physical identification document. Photographs and photocopies are not acceptable. Remote online notarization handles identity differently, through credential analysis and identity proofing.

posts.title: What Happens If Your Florida Notary Commission Expires?
posts.metaTitle: Expired Florida Notary Commission: There Is No Grace Period
posts.metaDesc: A Florida notary commission ends the day it expires. Notarizations performed after that date are void, and there is no grace period — here is what to do.
posts.excerpt: The commission ends at midnight on the expiration date. There is nothing after it.

sections.html:
A Florida notary commission runs four years under Fla. Stat. §117.01 and ends on the expiration date printed on your certificate and stamped on your seal. There is no grace period, no probationary window, and no retroactive renewal.

The day after expiration you are not a notary. Any notarial act performed after that date is void — not defective, not curable by a corrective certificate, void. And performing one is the practice of a public office you do not hold.

If you are also registered as an online notary, note the second trap: RON registration is tied to the underlying commission. When the commission lapses, the online registration lapses with it, even if you paid for a longer RON platform subscription.

sections.h: What to do if you have already lapsed
sections.html:
1. Stop notarizing immediately. Not after the current appointment. Now.
  2. Apply as a new applicant. A lapsed commission is not renewed; it is replaced. You file a fresh application through a bonding agency, post a new $7,500 bond, and pay the fees again.
  3. Order a new seal. Your commission number changes. The old seal is now evidence of an expired commission and should be destroyed, not kept.
  4. Re-register for RON if you perform online notarizations, including the $25,000 RON bond and $25,000 E&O under §117.225.
  5. Deal with anything you notarized after the date. Tell the parties. A void notarization on a recorded instrument is a title problem, and it is far cheaper to fix in week one than in year three.

Commissions expire on a rolling four-year cycle, which means the date is almost never memorable and almost always inconvenient. Two habits solve it:

  • Start renewal at 90 days out. Processing takes weeks, and your bonding agency needs lead time. Ninety days is comfortable; thirty is not.
  • Set three calendar alerts — 90, 60, and 30 days before expiration — the day your new commission arrives. Do it once, and you never think about it again.

Your commission expiration date is printed on your certificate, appears on your seal, and is published in the Florida Department of State's records. If you are not certain of yours, look it up before you notarize anything else — you can search the register here, free.

faqs.q: Is there a grace period for an expired Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: No. A Florida notary commission ends on its expiration date. There is no grace period, and any notarial act performed after that date is void.

faqs.q: Can I renew a Florida notary commission after it expires?
faqs.a: Not as a renewal. Once the commission lapses you must apply as a new applicant — a new application through a bonding agency, a new $7,500 bond, new fees, and a new seal with your new commission number.

faqs.q: What happens to documents I notarized after my commission expired?
faqs.a: They are void, because you had no authority to perform the act. Notify the affected parties promptly. On a recorded instrument this can create a title defect that is far cheaper to cure immediately than later.

faqs.q: Does my RON registration survive my commission expiring?
faqs.a: No. Florida online notary registration is tied to the underlying notary commission. When the commission lapses the RON registration lapses with it, and you must re-register with a new $25,000 RON bond and E&O coverage.

faqs.q: When should I start renewing my Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: About 90 days before expiration. Processing and bonding take weeks, and starting at 30 days routinely leaves notaries with a gap in which they cannot lawfully work.

posts.title: The Loan Signing Package, Document by Document
posts.metaTitle: Loan Signing Documents Explained: Every Major Document and What the Notary Does
posts.metaDesc: A refinance package runs 100–150 pages, but only a handful of documents get notarized. Here is what each one is, which need a notary, and where signing agents go wrong.
keywords: what documents are in a loan package
posts.excerpt: Most of the package is disclosure. A short list gets notarized — know which, and why.

sections.html:
In a typical Florida refinance or purchase package, the notarized documents are a small subset:

  • Mortgage (or Deed of Trust in other states — Florida uses a mortgage). The security instrument that gets recorded. Acknowledgment. This is the document that must be perfect, because it goes on the public record.
  • Deed — on a purchase, the seller's conveyance. Acknowledgment, plus two subscribing witnesses under Fla. Stat. §689.01.
  • Signature/Name Affidavit — the borrower swears to name variations. Usually a jurat.
  • Occupancy Affidavit — sworn statement of intent to occupy. Jurat.
  • Compliance / Correction Agreement — the borrower agrees to correct clerical errors. Frequently notarized.
  • Errors and Omissions / Limited Power of Attorney — where present, almost always acknowledged.

Everything else — the Note, the Closing Disclosure, the disclosures, the escrow documents — is signed but usually not notarized. The Note is arguably the most important document in the package and typically carries no notarial certificate at all.

sections.h: The rest of the package, in plain terms
sections.html:
• Promissory Note — the borrower's promise to repay. Terms, rate, payment. Not usually notarized. Never let a borrower sign this one incorrectly; it is the debt itself.
  • Closing Disclosure (CD) — the five-page federal form with the loan terms and the final numbers. Borrowers ask about this one more than everything else combined.
  • Right of Rescission — on an owner-occupied refinance, a three-business-day window to cancel. Two copies per borrower, and the dates must be exactly right.
  • Truth in Lending / Loan Estimate — cost disclosures.
  • Escrow / Impound documents — how taxes and insurance are collected.
  • Flood, PMI, servicing disclosures — informational; sign and move.
  • Borrower's Certification and Authorization — permission to verify employment and credit.
  • First Payment Letter — when and where the first payment goes.

sections.h: Where signing agents actually go wrong
sections.html:
• Missing witnesses on the deed. Florida requires two subscribing witnesses on a conveyance. The notary may be one only if the notary actually observed the signing, and a second is still required. Arrange this before you leave the house.
  • Rescission dates. The three-day count excludes Sundays and federal holidays, and the transaction date, the expiration date, and the borrower's copies all have to agree.
  • Blank notarial certificates. Fill it before you stamp, every time — §117.05(4) sets out everything it must contain.
  • Answering “what does this mean.” Point to it, read it aloud, refer the question. Explaining it is legal advice a non-attorney notary may not give.
  • Missed initials. Page through the whole package before you leave. It costs two minutes and prevents almost every re-signing.

faqs.q: Which documents in a loan package get notarized?
faqs.a: Typically the mortgage, the deed on a purchase, and sworn affidavits such as the signature/name affidavit and occupancy affidavit. The promissory note and the Closing Disclosure are signed but usually not notarized.

faqs.q: Does the promissory note need to be notarized?
faqs.a: Usually not. The note is the borrower's promise to repay and generally carries no notarial certificate. The mortgage — the security instrument that gets recorded — is the document that is notarized.

faqs.q: How many documents are in a loan signing package?
faqs.a: Commonly 100–150 pages, though only a handful carry notarial certificates. Refinances tend to run longer than purchases because of the rescission documents.

faqs.q: Do Florida mortgages need witnesses?
faqs.a: Deeds require two subscribing witnesses under Fla. Stat. §689.01. Mortgages are treated differently — see §697.02 and §695.26(1)(f). Follow whatever the closing instructions specify for the particular instrument.

faqs.q: Can a signing agent explain the Closing Disclosure?
faqs.a: No. A notary who is not an attorney may not explain a document's legal effect. The signing agent may identify where a figure appears and read it aloud, then refer the borrower to the loan officer or closing agent.

posts.title: Florida Notary Application: Step by Step
posts.metaTitle: How to Apply for a Florida Notary Commission: The Complete Step-by-Step Process
posts.metaDesc: Application, education, bond, fees, and seal — the whole Florida notary commission process in order, with what each step actually costs and how long it takes.
keywords: how to apply to be a notary in florida
posts.excerpt: Six steps, one bonding agency, and about four to six weeks.

sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §117.01(1) sets the eligibility bar, and it is low:

  • At least 18 years of age
  • A legal resident of Florida — and you must remain one for the whole four-year term
  • A U.S. citizen, or a permanent resident alien who files a recorded Declaration of Domicile
  • Able to read, write, and understand English

Felony convictions must be disclosed on the application. A conviction is not automatically disqualifying, but civil rights must have been restored.

1. Complete the 3-hour education course. Required for first-time applicants only — three hours of interactive or classroom instruction covering notary duties and electronic notarization, from a state-approved vendor. Renewing notaries are exempt.
  2. Choose a bonding agency. Florida routes applications through bonding agencies rather than direct filing. The agency issues your $7,500 bond, submits the application to the state, and usually bundles the seal, journal, and E&O. You may use any approved agency — and the bundled prices vary widely, so compare.
  3. Complete the application. Personal information, the felony disclosure, and the oath of office. Your name must appear exactly as you want it on your commission and seal, because that is what you will sign as for four years.
  4. Post the $7,500 bond. Required by §117.01(7)(a) before you may execute the duties of the office and throughout the term. The bond protects the public, not you.
  5. Pay the fees. A $25 application fee, a $10 commission fee, and a $4 surcharge go to the state, with certain veteran exceptions. The bonding agency's own charge and the bond premium are on top of that.
  6. Receive your commission and order your seal. The certificate arrives with your commission number and expiration date. Your seal must carry the words “Notary Public-State of Florida,” your name, the expiration date, and the commission number, in photographically reproducible black ink under §117.05(3)(a).

sections.h: Timeline, cost, and the two decisions that matter
sections.html:
Timeline: the education course is one afternoon. Application processing typically runs two to four weeks after the bonding agency submits it. Budget four to six weeks from start to holding your seal, and do not accept work before the commission is in hand.

Cost: $39 in state fees, plus the bond premium, agency fee, education, seal, and journal. A bundled package generally lands between $80 and $150 depending on what is included and how much E&O you add.

Two decisions inside the process are worth thinking about rather than defaulting:

  • How much E&O to buy. Florida does not require it. Title companies effectively do — commonly $25,000 minimum and often $100,000 for loan signing work. Buying $10,000 to save $30 is a false economy if you intend to do closings.
  • Whether to register for RON now or later. Remote online notarization requires separate registration plus a $25,000 RON bond and $25,000 in E&O under §117.225. It is not part of the base commission and can be added at any time.

faqs.q: How do I become a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: Confirm you meet the §117.01 eligibility requirements, complete the 3-hour education course if you are a first-time applicant, apply through a bonding agency, post a $7,500 bond, pay the state fees, and order a seal once your commission arrives.

faqs.q: Do I have to use a bonding agency to apply?
faqs.a: In practice yes. Florida routes notary applications through bonding agencies, which issue the required $7,500 bond and submit the application. You may choose any approved agency, and their bundled package prices differ significantly.

faqs.q: How much are the Florida notary state fees?
faqs.a: A $25 application fee, a $10 commission fee, and a $4 surcharge, with exceptions for certain veterans. The bond premium, agency fee, education, seal, and journal are separate.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: Typically four to six weeks from starting the education course to receiving your commission and seal. Application processing after submission usually runs two to four weeks.

faqs.q: Is the 3-hour course required to renew a Florida notary commission?
faqs.a: No. The three-hour education requirement applies to first-time applicants only. Renewing notaries are not required to repeat it.

posts.title: Onboarding a Notary: A Title Company Checklist
posts.metaTitle: Notary Onboarding Checklist for Title Companies: What to Verify and What to Keep on File
posts.metaDesc: A practical onboarding file for title and escrow operations: what to verify before a notary touches a borrower's package, and what to re-verify on a schedule.
posts.excerpt: Built for closers and post-closers who need a defensible vendor file, not a longer form.

sections.html:
Everything below should exist as a document in the vendor file, not as a note that someone checked it.

  • Commission verification. Full legal name, commission number, issue and expiration dates, verified against the Florida Department of State record — not against the notary's own statement or a screenshot they supplied.
  • Government photo identification matching the commissioned name exactly.
  • Background screening report, dated. Most lender vendor-management policies require it current within 12 months; some require the screening to meet a specified standard.
  • E&O certificate of insurance showing carrier, limit, and expiration. $25,000 minimum is common; $100,000 is typical for loan signing work. If your policy requires it, confirm you are named as an additional interest.
  • RON registration status, if applicable — separate from the base commission, with its own $25,000 bond and E&O under Fla. Stat. §117.225.
  • W-9 and payment details.
  • Signed confidentiality and NPI handling acknowledgment. The notary is handling borrower nonpublic personal information; the acknowledgment is what makes your policy enforceable against them.
  • Coverage profile — counties, radius, evenings, weekends, same-day, printer capability, RON capability.

Onboarding is a snapshot. The two facts most likely to go stale are the two that matter most.

  • Commission expiration — quarterly. Florida commissions run four years on a rolling cycle, so expirations land unpredictably across your bench. A notarization performed on a lapsed commission is void, and on a recorded mortgage that is a title problem, not a scheduling problem.
  • E&O expiration — at policy renewal. Diary the date from the certificate; policies lapse quietly.
  • Background screening — annually, or at whatever interval your lender clients require.
  • Coverage profile — annually. Notaries move, buy printers, add RON, and stop taking evenings.

State Notary Agent publishes a free register built from the Florida Department of State's own published journals, showing commission numbers and expiration dates. It is the fastest way to run a quarterly sweep of your bench without filing anything.

sections.h: The part most onboarding forms miss
sections.html:
Credentials tell you a notary is permitted to do the work. They tell you nothing about whether the package comes back clean. Three questions at onboarding predict that better than any document:

  • “Walk me through what you do if the borrower's ID is expired when you arrive.” The right answer is: stop, call the closer, do not proceed. An agent who improvises here will improvise elsewhere.
  • “What do you say when a borrower asks what their interest rate means?” The right answer points to the document and refers the question. Anything that sounds like an explanation is a liability you are importing.
  • “What time do you scan back?” Same night is the only answer that does not eventually cost you a funding date.

Give feedback once when something goes wrong, specifically. Most notary errors are one-time; an agent told exactly what was defective rarely repeats it.

faqs.q: What should a title company verify before using a notary?
faqs.a: An active Florida commission verified against the Department of State record, government photo ID matching the commissioned name, a dated background screening, an E&O certificate with limit and expiration, RON registration if applicable, a W-9, and a signed confidentiality acknowledgment.

faqs.q: How often should a title company re-verify a notary's commission?
faqs.a: Quarterly is a reasonable cadence. Florida commissions run four years on a rolling cycle, so expirations fall unpredictably, and a notarization performed on a lapsed commission is void.

faqs.q: What E&O limit should a title company require?
faqs.a: $25,000 is a common minimum; $100,000 is typical for loan signing work. Some operations also require being named as an additional interest on the policy.

faqs.q: Does a notary's RON registration come with the regular commission?
faqs.a: No. Florida remote online notary registration is separate, and carries its own $25,000 bond and at least $25,000 in E&O coverage under Fla. Stat. §117.225. Verify it separately.

faqs.q: How can I check a Florida notary's commission for free?
faqs.a: Check the name, commission number, and expiration against the Florida Department of State's records. State Notary Agent's free register is compiled from the Department's published journals and shows commission numbers and expiration dates.

posts.title: How to Look Up a Florida Notary Commission
posts.metaTitle: Florida Notary Commission Lookup: How to Verify a Notary Is Real and Active
posts.metaDesc: Verifying a Florida notary takes about thirty seconds and prevents a void notarization. Here is what to check, where, and what a mismatch means.
posts.excerpt: Four fields to check, and one of them catches almost every problem.

sections.html:
A Florida notary commission is a public record. You do not need permission, a reason, or an account to verify one. Four fields, checked together:

  • Name — exactly as it appears on the seal. Not a nickname, not a maiden name.
  • Commission number — the identifier on the seal, usually beginning with two letters.
  • Expiration date — the field that catches almost every real problem.
  • Status — active, expired, or resigned.

The expiration date is the one that matters. Florida commissions run four years with no grace period. A notarization performed one day past expiration is void, and on a recorded deed or mortgage that becomes a title defect long after everyone has forgotten the appointment.

The Florida Department of State maintains the official record at notaries.dos.fl.gov. This is the authoritative source and the one to cite if anything is ever disputed.

This register — State Notary Agent — is a free searchable copy compiled from the Department's own published Notaries Public journals, showing name, commission series and number, issue and expiration dates, bonding agency, city, county, and ZIP. It is faster to search by name or city, and it is free. It is not the official record; when it matters legally, confirm against the Department.

One thing you will notice: neither source publishes a phone number or street address. Florida law protects those, and records flagged with an address restriction under Fla. Stat. §119.071(4)(d) — which covers judges, prosecutors, and law enforcement, among others — are withheld entirely.

• Name differs slightly. Often a legal name change that has not propagated. Ask. A notary must notarize under the exact commissioned name, so a seal that does not match the commission is a genuine problem.
  • Commission number not found. Verify you read the seal correctly, then treat it seriously. There is no reason a valid commission number should be absent from the state record.
  • Expired. The notarization is void. If a document has already been recorded, contact the title company or closing agent immediately — a corrective instrument early is inexpensive; a title claim later is not.
  • Not found at all. Do not proceed. Anyone can buy a rubber stamp.

If you are a title company or lender verifying a bench of notaries rather than one, run the check on a schedule. Expirations arrive on a rolling four-year cycle, so there is no single date to watch.

faqs.q: How do I verify a Florida notary is legitimate?
faqs.a: Check the name, commission number, and expiration date from the seal against the Florida Department of State's notary records. All four fields should match, and the status should be active.

faqs.q: Is a Florida notary commission public record?
faqs.a: Yes. Commission information is a public record, though street addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth are not published, and records with an address restriction under Fla. Stat. §119.071(4)(d) are withheld.

faqs.q: What if the notary's commission was expired when they notarized my document?
faqs.a: The notarization is void — Florida has no grace period. Contact the title company, closing agent, or receiving party immediately. On a recorded instrument this is a title issue that gets more expensive the longer it sits.

faqs.q: Can I look up a Florida notary by name for free?
faqs.a: Yes. The Florida Department of State maintains the official searchable record, and State Notary Agent publishes a free register compiled from the Department's own published journals, searchable by name, city, county, or commission number.

faqs.q: Why can't I find a notary's phone number in the state records?
faqs.a: Florida does not publish notaries' phone numbers, street addresses, or dates of birth. Only name, commission details, bonding agency, and general location are public.

posts.title: Can a Florida Notary Certify a Copy?
posts.metaTitle: Can a Florida Notary Certify a Copy? Attested Photocopies and What's Off Limits
posts.metaDesc: Florida notaries may attest that a photocopy is a true copy — but not of a vital record, and not of a public record the custodian can copy. Here is the rule.
keywords: can a notary copy a birth certificate
posts.excerpt: Yes for your passport. No for your birth certificate. The line is statutory.

sections.html:
Under Fla. Stat. §117.05(12), a Florida notary may supervise the making of a photocopy of an original document and attest to the trueness of the copy. This is called an attested photocopy, and it is a real notarial act.

The mechanics matter. The notary must personally supervise the copying — meaning the original is presented to the notary and the copy is made under the notary's observation. A notary may not attest to a copy someone brings in already made, no matter how obviously accurate it looks.

The notary then completes a certificate stating that the copy is a true and correct copy of the original presented, dates it, signs it, and seals it.

The same subsection carves out two categories, and they cover most of what people actually ask for:

  • Vital records. Birth certificates, death certificates, and marriage certificates. A notary may not attest to a copy of any of these. Certified copies come from the issuing vital records office, and only from there.
  • Public records, where the custodian can make a copy. Court records, recorded deeds, property records, and anything else held by a government custodian who issues certified copies. If the clerk can certify it, the notary may not.

The logic is straightforward: a notary's attestation would be a lesser substitute for a certified copy from the office that holds the record. Receiving agencies know this, which is why a notarized copy of a birth certificate gets rejected even when a notary was willing to make one.

Diplomas, transcripts, and school records sit in a gray zone that depends on whether the issuing institution is a public custodian. When in doubt, the issuing institution is the safer route.

sections.h: What you can actually get attested — and the alternative
sections.html:
Commonly and lawfully attested: passports, driver licenses, Social Security cards, immigration documents held by the individual, private contracts, wills, powers of attorney, medical records already in your possession, insurance policies, and personal correspondence. In short: documents you hold, that no government custodian is standing by to certify.

When a notary cannot help, use a copy certification by document custodian. The person who holds the original signs a sworn statement that the attached copy is a true copy of a document in their possession, and the notary notarizes that statement as a jurat. The notary is certifying the affiant's oath, not the copy — which is entirely permissible, and is what many receiving agencies will actually accept.

Before you drive anywhere: ask the receiving party what they will accept. “Notarized copy” is used loosely, and half the time what they need is a certified copy from the issuing office instead.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary certify a copy of a document?
faqs.a: Yes, for most private documents. Under Fla. Stat. §117.05(12) a notary may supervise the making of a photocopy and attest that it is a true copy — but not of a vital record, and not of a public record the custodian can copy.

faqs.q: Can a notary copy my birth certificate?
faqs.a: No. Birth certificates are vital records, and Florida notaries may not attest to copies of them. A certified copy must be obtained from the vital records office that issued it.

faqs.q: Can a notary certify a copy of a recorded deed?
faqs.a: No, if the county clerk or recorder can issue a certified copy. Florida notaries may not attest to copies of public records where the custodian can make one.

faqs.q: Can a notary attest to a copy of my passport?
faqs.a: Yes. A passport is a document in your possession and is not a vital record, so a Florida notary may supervise the copying and attest that the copy is true and correct.

faqs.q: What is a copy certification by document custodian?
faqs.a: The holder of the original signs a sworn statement that the attached copy is a true copy of a document in their possession, and the notary notarizes that statement as a jurat. The notary certifies the oath, not the copy — a lawful workaround many agencies accept.

posts.title: What Happens to Your Commission If You Move Out of Florida?
posts.metaTitle: Moving Out of Florida: What Happens to Your Notary Commission
posts.metaDesc: Florida residency is a continuing requirement, not a one-time box on the application. Move away and the commission ends — here is what you owe the state on the way out.
keywords: move out of state notary commission
posts.excerpt: Residency is a condition of holding the office, not just of getting it.

sections.html:
Fla. Stat. §117.01(1) requires a notary to be a legal resident of Florida. That requirement runs for the entire four-year term — it is not satisfied once at application and then forgotten.

When you cease to be a Florida resident, you cease to be eligible to hold the office. The commission does not travel with you, does not convert to another state's commission, and does not sit dormant until you come back.

The practical trigger is establishing residency elsewhere: a new state's driver license, voter registration, homestead, or a declaration of domicile. Owning property in another state or spending a season there does not by itself end Florida residency. Moving does.

sections.h: What to do when you move
sections.html:
1. Stop notarizing on the Florida commission. Once you are no longer a Florida resident you are no longer eligible to act.
  2. Submit a written resignation to the Florida Department of State, and note the effective date.
  3. Destroy the seal. Not store it, not keep it as a souvenir. A seal in a drawer is an instrument someone else can misuse, and it remains associated with your name.
  4. Retain your records. If you performed remote online notarizations, the §117.245 obligation to maintain the electronic journal and recordings for at least 10 years does not end because your commission did. Arrange the repository before you move, and notify the Department within 30 days if you delegate retention.
  5. Apply in your new state. Requirements vary enormously — some states require an exam, some a longer bond, some no education at all. Nothing about your Florida commission carries over.

sections.h: The situations people actually ask about
sections.html:
• Snowbirds. If Florida remains your legal residence — license, voter registration, homestead — you are still a Florida resident and the commission stands. But you may only perform notarial acts while physically located in Florida. A Florida notary in Ohio in July is not a notary that day.
  • Military. Service members domiciled in Florida who are stationed elsewhere generally retain Florida residency. The physical-location limit on performing acts still applies.
  • RON and location. Remote online notarization changes where the signer may be, not where the notary may be. A Florida online notary must be physically located in Florida when performing the act, even though the signer may be anywhere.
  • Moving back. A resigned commission is not reinstated. You apply as a new applicant, with a new bond, new fees, and a new commission number.

faqs.q: What happens to my Florida notary commission if I move out of state?
faqs.a: You cease to be eligible to hold it. Florida residency under Fla. Stat. §117.01 is a continuing requirement for the whole four-year term. Stop notarizing, submit a written resignation to the Department of State, and destroy the seal.

faqs.q: Can I keep my Florida notary commission if I spend part of the year elsewhere?
faqs.a: Yes, if Florida remains your legal residence. But you may only perform notarial acts while physically located in Florida — a Florida notary cannot notarize while standing in another state.

faqs.q: Can a Florida RON notary perform online notarizations from another state?
faqs.a: No. Remote online notarization changes where the signer may be, not the notary. A Florida online notary must be physically located in Florida when performing the act.

faqs.q: Do I still have to keep my RON records after I resign?
faqs.a: Yes. The §117.245 requirement to retain the electronic journal and audio-video recordings for at least 10 years survives the end of the commission. Arrange a repository and notify the Department within 30 days if you delegate retention.

faqs.q: If I move back to Florida, can I get my old commission back?
faqs.a: No. A resigned commission is not reinstated. You apply as a new applicant, with a new bond, new fees, and a new commission number and seal.

posts.title: The Closing Disclosure at the Signing Table
posts.metaTitle: The Closing Disclosure and the Notary: What You May Point To and What You Must Not Explain
posts.metaDesc: The CD generates more borrower questions than the rest of the package combined — and it is the document where a signing agent is most likely to cross into legal advice.
posts.excerpt: Five pages, and the place where more signing agents get into trouble than anywhere else.

sections.html:
The Closing Disclosure is the five-page federal form delivered before closing that sets out the borrower's final loan terms and closing costs. Under federal rule, the borrower must receive it at least three business days before consummation — which is why the closer is often anxious about dates on this one specifically.

What is on it, page by page:

  • Page 1 — loan terms, projected payments, and costs at closing. Rate, monthly payment, whether any of it can increase.
  • Page 2 — the itemized closing cost table: origination, services the borrower shopped for and did not, taxes, prepaids, escrow.
  • Page 3 — calculating cash to close, and the summaries of transactions for borrower and seller.
  • Page 4 — additional information: assumption, escrow account, late payment, partial payments.
  • Page 5 — loan calculations, total of payments, APR, total interest percentage, and contact information.

The CD is signed but generally not notarized. Its presence in the package is disclosure, not execution.

A Florida notary who is not an attorney may not explain a document's legal effect. On the CD, the questions arrive constantly and they all sound reasonable.

You may: identify where an item appears, read the printed text aloud verbatim, state what the form itself labels a figure, and confirm the number matches what is printed.

You may not: explain what a term means, say whether a figure is correct or reasonable, compare it to the Loan Estimate, opine on whether the borrower should sign, or characterize a cost as normal, high, or a mistake.

The phrasing that works:

  • “Your interest rate is right here on page one — it reads 6.375%.”
  • “That line is labeled Total Closing Costs, and the figure printed is $8,412.”
  • “I'm not able to explain what that means — but that's exactly the right question for your loan officer, and I'm glad to pause while you call. I have the number right here.”

That last sentence is the whole job. Not a refusal — a redirect, with the phone number in your hand.

sections.h: When the borrower says the numbers are wrong
sections.html:
This happens, and how you handle it determines whether you ever get called by that title company again.

  1. Do not argue and do not reassure. You do not know whether the figure is wrong, and telling a borrower it is probably fine is both an opinion and a liability.
  2. Stop the signing. Do not have them sign the CD and “sort it out later.” Once signed, the leverage is gone.
  3. Call the closer or loan officer from the table. Hand the phone to the borrower. Ninety percent of the time it is resolved in four minutes — a figure the borrower was reading from an older estimate.
  4. If it cannot be resolved, end the appointment cleanly. Pack the package, tell the borrower the closer will follow up, and call the closer from the driveway. A rescheduled signing is a minor annoyance. A borrower who signs under protest is a lawsuit.
  5. Document it. Time, who you called, what was said, in your journal.

Closers do not remember the signings that went smoothly. They remember the agent who called before a problem became their problem.

faqs.q: Does the Closing Disclosure need to be notarized?
faqs.a: Usually not. The Closing Disclosure is signed as a federal disclosure but generally carries no notarial certificate. The mortgage and the sworn affidavits are the documents that get notarized.

faqs.q: Can a notary explain the Closing Disclosure to a borrower?
faqs.a: No. Explaining a document's legal effect is legal advice, which a Florida notary who is not an attorney may not give. A signing agent may point to where a figure appears and read the printed text aloud, then refer questions to the loan officer.

faqs.q: What should a signing agent do if the borrower says the numbers are wrong?
faqs.a: Stop the signing, do not reassure them, and call the closer or loan officer from the table so the borrower can speak to them directly. If it cannot be resolved, end the appointment and notify the closer immediately.

faqs.q: What is on each page of the Closing Disclosure?
faqs.a: Page 1: loan terms, projected payments, costs at closing. Page 2: itemized closing costs. Page 3: cash to close and transaction summaries. Page 4: additional loan information. Page 5: loan calculations, APR, and contacts.
