faqs.q: Why does the borrower have to get the Closing Disclosure three days early?
faqs.a: Federal rule requires delivery at least three business days before consummation so the borrower has time to review the final terms. That timing requirement is why closers are particular about dates on this document.

posts.title: Florida Notary Education Requirements
posts.metaTitle: Florida Notary Education Requirements: The 3-Hour Course, Who Needs It, and What Counts
posts.metaDesc: Florida requires three hours of instruction for first-time notary applicants — and nothing for renewals. Here is exactly what the requirement is, and what is being upsold on top of it.
posts.excerpt: Three hours, first-time applicants only. Everything beyond that is optional, and much of it is sold as though it isn't.

sections.html:
A first-time applicant for a Florida notary commission must complete at least three hours of interactive or classroom instruction covering the duties of a notary public, including electronic notarization. The course must be taken from a vendor approved by the state.

Three points that resolve most of the confusion:

  • It applies to first-time applicants only. Renewing notaries are not required to repeat it.
  • It covers electronic notarization, which is why the content mentions e-notarization even for applicants who never intend to do it.
  • There is no continuing education requirement for Florida notaries. None. Any course marketed as required annual notary CE is not describing Florida law.

The state publishes the list of approved education vendors — well over two dozen of them, including the National Notary Association, the American Society of Notaries, and a number of Florida-specific providers. Any approved vendor satisfies the requirement identically.

The syllabus is set to the duties of the office, and it is genuinely useful even to people who resent sitting through it:

  • The notarial acts — acknowledgments, jurats, oaths, attested copies, marriage solemnization
  • Identifying signers under Fla. Stat. §117.05(5), including credible witnesses
  • Completing the notarial certificate correctly under §117.05(4)
  • Seal requirements under §117.05(3)
  • Fees — the $10 cap and what falls outside it
  • Prohibited acts under §117.107, including the family-member restriction
  • The unauthorized practice of law line
  • Electronic and remote online notarization basics

Cost typically runs $20–$40 as a standalone, and it is frequently bundled into a bonding agency's application package at little or no additional charge. If you are paying substantially more than that for the bare requirement, you are paying for something else.

sections.h: What's optional — and which optional things are worth it
sections.html:
The notary education market sells a great deal on top of a three-hour requirement. Sorting it honestly:

  • Loan signing agent certification — not required by Florida, but practically useful. It teaches the loan documents and satisfies the onboarding checkbox most signing services use. Worth it if you intend to do closings; pointless otherwise.
  • RON training — not a statutory requirement, but most RON platforms require their own onboarding, and the technology genuinely has a learning curve. Usually included with the platform.
  • “Advanced” or “certified” notary designations — private titles with no legal standing in Florida. No borrower, title company, or court will ever ask.
  • Annual notary CE subscriptions — Florida requires none. Skip them.

The one investment that reliably pays is not a course at all. It is reading Chapter 117 once, straight through, and keeping the Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries within reach.

faqs.q: Is a course required to become a notary in Florida?
faqs.a: Yes, for first-time applicants: at least three hours of interactive or classroom instruction covering notary duties and electronic notarization, from a state-approved vendor.

faqs.q: Do I have to retake the notary course to renew in Florida?
faqs.a: No. The three-hour education requirement applies to first-time applicants only. Renewing Florida notaries are not required to repeat it.

faqs.q: Does Florida require notary continuing education?
faqs.a: No. Florida has no continuing education requirement for notaries. Any product marketed as mandatory annual notary CE in Florida is not describing state law.

faqs.q: How much does the Florida notary course cost?
faqs.a: Typically $20–$40 standalone, and it is often bundled into a bonding agency's application package at little or no extra cost.

faqs.q: Is loan signing agent certification required in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Florida requires only an active notary commission. Signing agent certification is a private credential that teaches loan documents and satisfies signing service onboarding requirements, but grants no legal authority.

posts.title: How to Verify a Notary Commission Before a Closing
posts.metaTitle: Verifying a Notary Commission Before a Closing: A Title Agent's Procedure
posts.metaDesc: A void notarization on a recorded mortgage is a title claim. Verification takes under a minute — here is the procedure, and when to run it.
posts.excerpt: Sixty seconds before the assignment beats a corrective instrument two years later.

sections.h: Why this is a title issue, not an admin task
sections.html:
A Florida notary commission runs four years, and Florida provides no grace period. A notarial act performed after the expiration date is void — the notary had no authority to perform it.

On a mortgage or deed, a void acknowledgment means the instrument was not properly executed for recording. That surfaces on a later title search, at the worst possible moment: someone else's closing, years after everyone involved has moved on. Curing it means locating the original signers and re-executing, or filing a corrective instrument — both of which cost more than the entire notary fee by orders of magnitude.

The expiration date is the field that catches this. Everything else on the verification is confirming that the notary is who they say they are.

1. Capture four fields from the seal or certificate: the notary's name exactly as printed, the commission number, the expiration date, and the date of the notarial act.
  2. Confirm the act date precedes the expiration date. This single comparison prevents nearly every void notarization.
  3. Match name and commission number against the state record. The Florida Department of State maintains the authoritative record at notaries.dos.fl.gov. State Notary Agent's free register, compiled from the Department's published journals, is faster for name and city searches during intake.
  4. Confirm the commissioned name matches the signature and printed name on the certificate. A notary must act under the exact commissioned name.
  5. For a RON act, verify online notary registration separately. It is distinct from the base commission and carries its own $25,000 bond and E&O requirement under Fla. Stat. §117.225.

• At onboarding — before a notary ever touches a borrower's package.
  • Quarterly across the whole bench — expirations arrive on a rolling four-year cycle, so there is no annual date to watch. A quarterly sweep of names against the register takes a few minutes and catches the notary whose commission lapsed in March.
  • Before any assignment where the notary has been dormant for six months or more.
  • In post-closing review, against the certificate as executed — verify the act date against the expiration printed on the seal. This is where a lapse is still cheap to fix.

Two additional checks worth building into the same pass: E&O expiration, diaried from the certificate of insurance, and background screening date, at whatever interval your lender clients require. Both lapse quietly, and both are what an audit asks for.

faqs.q: Why does a title company need to verify a notary's commission?
faqs.a: Because Florida has no grace period. A notarial act performed after the commission expires is void, and on a recorded mortgage or deed that becomes a title defect discovered years later at another closing.

faqs.q: What should I check when verifying a Florida notary?
faqs.a: The notary's name exactly as commissioned, the commission number, the expiration date, and the date of the notarial act — confirming the act date falls before expiration, and matching name and number against the state record.

faqs.q: How often should a title company re-verify its notary bench?
faqs.a: Quarterly. Florida commissions expire on a rolling four-year cycle, so there is no single annual date to watch, and a lapse can occur in any month.

faqs.q: Where is the official Florida notary record?
faqs.a: The Florida Department of State maintains the authoritative record. State Notary Agent's free register is compiled from the Department's published journals and is faster for name and city searches, but the Department is the record to cite if anything is disputed.

faqs.q: Does verifying a notary commission also verify RON authority?
faqs.a: No. Florida online notary registration is separate from the base commission and carries its own $25,000 bond and at least $25,000 in E&O coverage under Fla. Stat. §117.225. Verify it separately for any remote act.

posts.title: Can a Florida RON Notary Notarize for an Out-of-State Signer?
posts.metaTitle: RON and Out-of-State Signers: Where the Notary Must Be vs. Where the Signer May Be
posts.metaDesc: Yes — the signer can be anywhere. The notary cannot. Here is the rule that governs remote online notarization across state lines, and the acceptance question that actually decides it.
posts.excerpt: The notary's location governs. The signer's location almost never does.

sections.html:
A notary's authority comes from the state that commissioned them, and it operates where the notary is physically standing. That principle does not change with remote online notarization — RON changes how the signer appears, not where the notary may act.

So for a Florida online notary:

  • The notary must be physically located in Florida at the time of the notarial act. Not the notary's home state on paper — their physical location that day.
  • The signer may be anywhere — another state, another country — appearing by live two-way audio-video with credential analysis and identity proofing.
  • The act is a Florida notarial act, governed by Florida law, recorded in the Florida electronic journal, and subject to the §117.245 ten-year retention rule.

This is what makes RON genuinely useful for title work: a seller who has already relocated, a borrower deployed overseas, an investor closing in three states in one week, or an heir who lives eleven hundred miles from the property.

sections.h: The question that actually decides it
sections.html:
Legal authority is the easy part. The real constraint is acceptance, and it has three separate gates:

  • The receiving jurisdiction. Most states recognize a properly performed out-of-state notarial act, and many have specific provisions recognizing remote notarizations from other states. But recognition is a question of the receiving state's law, not Florida's.
  • The county recorder. A recorder that does not accept electronic seals, or does not e-record, is a practical blocker regardless of what the statutes permit.
  • The lender and title underwriter. This is where most RON transactions actually die. Investor guidelines and underwriter policy frequently restrict RON by loan type, occupancy, or state — and they change.

Confirm all three before the appointment is scheduled, not at it. “Florida law permits this” is not an answer to “will the underwriter insure it.”

If you are the notary: verify your own physical location, not just your residency, and do not take a RON session from a hotel in Georgia. Confirm the signer's ID will pass credential analysis — foreign identity documents frequently do not. And remember the fee: the RON act itself is capped at $25 under Fla. Stat. §117.275, though a signing-agent service fee is separate.

If you are the title company: confirm underwriter approval for the specific transaction, confirm the recorder accepts electronic recording for that instrument, and confirm witness requirements are satisfiable remotely — Florida deeds require two subscribing witnesses under §689.01, and how they participate in a RON session has to be worked out in advance rather than discovered at the appointment.

If you are the signer: you need a government photo ID that passes automated credential analysis, a device with a working camera and microphone, and a stable connection. Identity proofing uses knowledge-based questions drawn from public and credit records — and there are limited attempts.

faqs.q: Can a Florida notary notarize for someone in another state using RON?
faqs.a: Yes. The signer may be anywhere; the notary must be physically located in Florida at the time of the act. The result is a Florida notarial act governed by Florida law.

faqs.q: Can a Florida RON notary work from outside Florida?
faqs.a: No. The notary must be physically present in Florida when performing the notarial act. Remote online notarization changes the signer's location requirement, not the notary's.

faqs.q: Will other states accept a Florida remote online notarization?
faqs.a: Usually, but recognition is governed by the receiving state's law, and acceptance also depends on the county recorder and — for loans — the lender and title underwriter. Confirm all three before scheduling.

faqs.q: Can a signer outside the United States use Florida RON?
faqs.a: Often yes, provided their identification passes credential analysis and identity proofing, and the connection supports live audio-video. Foreign identity documents frequently fail automated credential analysis, so test in advance.

faqs.q: How much does a Florida remote online notarization cost?
faqs.a: The notarial act itself is capped at $25 under Fla. Stat. §117.275. A separate signing-agent or closing service fee may apply and is not subject to that cap.
